reconstruction.proof:
Put δ=(i/(2π))∂bar∂. The first assertion is exactly the supplied Proposition 2.9, with its hypotheses unchanged: u is bounded and plurisubharmonic on the open set in question. For a locally bounded u, apply it on relatively compact smaller open sets. The definitions agree on overlaps because distributional differentiation and multiplication by the prescribed bounded representative are local operations. This proves the localization assertion.

The assertion concerning continuous potentials is precisely the supplied Proposition 2.3. In particular, its topology is locally uniform convergence, and its domain consists of continuous plurisubharmonic potentials. No decreasing-convergence assertion for discontinuous limits is inferred from it. The analytic-set assertion is the supplied Corollary 2.5, applied on a countable coordinate cover; continuity of u is retained at every application.

Since D=4πδ, induction in the recursive definition gives T_k^D=(4π)^k T_k^δ. The same argument works for mixed recursively defined products. Multiplication by a fixed bounded Borel representative does not change this scalar factor. Consequently the equation rescales by (4π)^−n, exactly as stated.

Finally δu=(i/(2π))Σ u_{j bar k} dz_j∧dbar z_k. Taking its nth exterior power gives n! det(u_{j bar k}) times the product of the diagonal coordinate forms. Since i dz_j∧dbar z_j=2 dx_j∧dy_j, that product is π^−n dλ. Thus (δu)^n=n!π^−n det(u_{j bar k})dλ. These computations use ordinary coordinate volume and no divided-volume factorial.

notes.text:
A CIRCULAR-LIFT PROOF OF WEIGHTED DECREASING CONVERGENCE.

The purpose is to remove the specifically weighted convergence theorem from the external-input list in n3. Assume only the ordinary foundational Bedford–Taylor statement: locally uniformly bounded decreasing psh sequences have weakly convergent unweighted products, with the product of the limiting functions as limit. Mixed products follow from single-sequence products by polarization of positive sums. The extra-dimensional argument below proves the needed weighted variant, including the exact normalization.

Lemma. On a ball B in C^m let a_j and b_{1,j},…,b_{m,j} be locally uniformly bounded decreasing psh sequences, with limits a and b_1,…,b_m. Put
μ_j=dd^cb_{1,j}∧…∧dd^cb_{m,j}, μ=dd^cb_1∧…∧dd^cb_m.
Then a_jμ_j→aμ weakly on compact subsets. Smooth fixed coefficient factors and products of lower degree follow by wedging with dummy fixed flat psh potentials and testing current coefficients.

Proof. Work on a relatively compact base ball B' so every a_j and a lies between constants L and U. Choose 0<r<R with log r^2<L−1 and log R^2>U+1. On B'×{|w|<R}, define
v_j(z,w)=max{a_j(z),log|w|^2},
v(z,w)=max{a(z),log|w|^2}.
These are psh, locally uniformly bounded (including at w=0 because of the a_j lower bound), and v_j decreases to v. The b_{r,j} are pulled back independently of w. Therefore the ordinary unweighted mixed decreasing theorem in complex dimension m+1 gives
T_j=μ_j∧dd^cv_j → T=μ∧dd^cv.

We claim a direct distributional formula for these currents, which does not itself use weighted convergence. The defining bounded-product recursion gives
μ∧dd^cv=dd^c(vμ)
and likewise for μ_j. The current μ has top bidegree (m,m) in the z variables. Thus all terms of dd^c involving a z differential vanish by bidegree; only the vertical dd^c_w survives. Equivalently this equality can be verified by testing and Fubini in the w variable, with μ a finite measure on compact subsets. For every fixed z, the vertical function is
w↦max{a(z),log|w|^2}.
With dd^c=(i/(2π))∂bar∂, dd^c log|w|^2 is unit point mass at 0. Hence
 dd^c_w max{t,log|w|^2}
is unit probability mass uniformly distributed on the circle |w|=e^{t/2}. To check the coefficient without relying on convention: for a radial smooth test, integrate the planar Laplacian of the piecewise harmonic function; its outward radial derivative jumps from 0 to 2/r at the circle, so the total Euclidean Laplacian mass is 4π, and dd^c is (1/(4π)) times Euclidean Laplacian measure. The resulting mass is exactly one.

Consequently
T=∫_{z∈B'} [probability circle at |w|=e^{a(z)/2}] dμ(z),
and the identical formula holds for T_j with a_j,μ_j. This formula is meaningful for the bounded canonical Borel representatives, including if μ charges a discontinuity set: it follows from the distribution dd^c_w(vμ) and Fubini, not from an assumed continuity of a.

Choose a smooth radial compactly supported function θ(w) on the annulus {r<|w|<R} which equals log|w|^2 on a neighborhood of every circle with radius between e^{L/2} and e^{U/2}. For a smooth compactly supported base test ξ(z),
⟨T_j,ξ(z)θ(w)⟩=∫B' ξ a_j dμ_j,
⟨T,ξ(z)θ(w)⟩=∫B' ξ a dμ.
The unweighted convergence T_j→T proves the claimed weighted convergence. Local mass bounds and the uniform bound on a_j extend the test class to continuous compactly supported ξ if desired.

This also proves variants in which the weighted psh sequence and the psh sequences defining the measure are different. For a quasi-psh weight, add a fixed smooth psh quadratic locally, apply the lemma, then subtract its unweighted smooth contribution. For lower-degree currents in base dimension d, wedge with fixed flat dd^c potentials to reach top degree; polarization of such test factors, together with scalar test functions, recovers all current coefficients. For smoothly varying fixed coefficient forms, uniform convergence of the coefficients and uniform local masses allow replacement by their limit.

APPLICATION TO N3. The convolved U_j+b r_j^2 plus a fixed local quadratic is a bounded decreasing psh sequence. All positive closed currents in the expansion of A_j^2 are dd^c of such bounded decreasing psh functions (or fixed flat quadratic potentials). Thus the lemma proves precisely the weighted convergence of ∫U_jA_j^2 used in the rough energy proof. No separate weighted BT theorem is now needed. The ordinary unweighted mixed decreasing theorem in one extra dimension suffices, and mixed convergence itself reduces by polarization to the usual single-sequence theorem. All hypotheses—local uniform bounds, genuine decreasing canonical limits, and psh rather than merely positive nonclosed currents—have been explicitly arranged.

Remaining bibliographic issue: this proof removes the need to locate an explicit weighted theorem in the primary Bedford–Taylor papers. The only foundational convergence source still needing a literal primary-text audit is the ordinary unweighted decreasing theorem. This note does not claim to have carried out that literal audit.

reconstruction.proof:
Here is a derivation from ordinary decreasing continuity that does not assume the desired weighted convergence. First, ordinary mixed decreasing continuity follows by polarization: for nonnegative constants t_i, Σt_i b_{i,j} decreases to the locally bounded canonical plurisubharmonic function Σt_i b_i. Apply the declared power-continuity premise and recover each mixed product from finitely many such powers. This argument works in every dimension and degree permitted by the premise.

We next prove weighted convergence for top-degree positive measures on a domain in C^d. Write P_j=δb_{1,j}∧...∧δb_{d,j}. Locally all a_j and a lie in a fixed finite interval [−N,N]. Add a complex variable t and, for an integer l≥1, set c_j(z,t)=exp(l a_j(z)+Re t). These are locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions decreasing to c=exp(l a+Re t). Regard P_j as a current on the product domain. Mixed unweighted decreasing continuity, just established in dimension d+1, gives δc_j∧P_j→δc∧P.

The defining recursive identity for these ordinary products identifies this convergence explicitly. Because P_j has top degree in z and is closed,
δ(c_j P_j)=(i/(8π))exp(l a_j(z)+Re t) P_j∧dt∧dbar t.
All z-differentiation terms vanish by degree. This identity follows distributionally by differentiation only in t; c_jP_j is multiplication by its canonical bounded Borel representative. The same identity holds at the limit. Testing against φ(z)χ(t), with a nonnegative compactly supported χ having positive integral against exp(Re t)i dt∧dbar t, proves exp(l a_j)P_j→exp(l a)P. The case l=0 is ordinary unweighted convergence. Thus no weighted continuity theorem has been inserted into this argument: the recursion is the definition of the ordinary mixed products.

Polynomials approximate log x uniformly on [exp(−N),exp(N)]. Applying the preceding result to the powers exp(l a_j), and using the locally uniformly bounded masses of P_j supplied by their weak convergence, gives a_jP_j→aP. The approximation error is at most its uniform scalar error times a uniformly bounded local mass.

For degree r<d, wedge the currents with fixed products of d−r constant positive (1,1)-forms, each the Hessian of a smooth positive quadratic. The preceding top-degree argument applies with these additional stationary plurisubharmonic factors. Such products span the real vector space of constant (d−r,d−r)-forms, by polarization of rank-one positive (1,1)-forms. Testing their coefficients against arbitrary smooth scalar test functions proves convergence of every current coefficient. This proves the lower-degree assertion, not merely its trace.

Positive currents have coefficient variations bounded locally by a constant times their trace measure. Together with the common bound on the weights, this gives uniform local variation bounds. Multiplication by fixed smooth coefficient forms is therefore valid; replacing those forms by locally uniformly converging forms changes the pairing by a quantity tending to zero. A quasi-plurisubharmonic weight with a common smooth quadratic shift is handled by applying the result to its plurisubharmonic shift and subtracting the fixed smooth quadratic times the ordinarily convergent currents.

In the stated torus application the assumed shifts U_j+b r_j²+q are decreasing bounded plurisubharmonic sequences. Expanding A_j² as prescribed, apply the result term by term, subtracting q+b r_j² from the weight. The b r_j² contribution tends to zero by the same variation bounds. This proves U_jA_j²→UA². A finite partition of unity on the compact torus then gives convergence of the integrals.

notes.detailedSummary: Let C be obtained from an elliptic curve E1 by replacing a coordinate disk at p by the cusp y^2=x^3, using z↦(z^2,z^3). Its normalization E1→C is finite, degree one, and a homeomorphism. X=C×E2 is compact, reduced, connected, pure dimensional, locally irreducible, and has complex dimension two. A background h0=hC+κ2 is ambient-smooth and positive; on Y=E1×E2 its pullback H0=η+κ2 is closed and degenerates along {p}×E2. notes.text:
CONSTRUCTION AND GEOMETRY. Throughout dd^c=(i/(2π))∂bar∂, and d^c=(i/(4π))(bar∂−∂), so dd^c=d d^c.

1. The singular compact curve. Fix elliptic curves E1=C/Λ1 and E2=C/Λ2, and a point p∈E1. Choose a holomorphic coordinate z centered at p on a small disk. Replace that disk by the reduced cusp chart {y^2=x^3}, identified on the punctured disk by x=z^2,y=z^3. Glue the punctured cusp chart to E1\{p} by this identification. The resulting compact complex curve C has underlying topological space E1. Its only singularity q is a cusp. Its local ring at q is C{z^2,z^3}, which is a domain and has one analytic branch. The map π1:E1→C is finite: locally z is integral over C{z^2,z^3}, since z^2=x, and globally the map is proper. It is degree one and bijective, hence a homeomorphism. It is the normalization, and is an isomorphism away from p.

Set X=C×E2 and Y=E1×E2, with π=π1×id. Then X is compact, connected, reduced, pure of dimension two, and locally irreducible. Its singular locus is the elliptic curve {q}×E2. Y is a smooth compact complex torus and π is a resolution in the sense of a proper smooth birational model, although here it is finite. This is a cuspidal pinching construction, not a projective-cone construction.

2. A positive local-embedding background. Choose a smooth Hermitian form hC on C in the local-embedding sense. It can be constructed by finite chart partitions from positive ambient Euclidean forms. Near q take specifically hC=dd^c(|x|^2+|y|^2)|C. Away from q use positive forms on the smooth curve and glue with smooth local-embedding partitions; on the overlap all tangent metrics are positive and positive ambient extensions can be retained. Let κj be fixed flat positive (1,1)-forms on Ej. Put η=π1*hC. This is a smooth nonnegative form on E1, positive away from p, and near p
η=(i/(2π))(4|z|^2+9|z|^4) dz∧dbar z.
In particular it vanishes at p; this degeneracy must not be ignored. Write η=ρκ1, with ρ smooth, ρ≥0, ρ>0 outside p. Set λ=(∫E1η)/(∫E1κ1)>0.

The product background h0=prC*hC+prE2*κ2 is positive in the local-embedding sense on X. Its pullback H0=η+κ2 is smooth, nonnegative, and closed on Y, but has rank one along D={p}×E2.

3. A nonclosed pluriclosed perturbation. Choose a real smooth function A on C whose support is contained in Creg and misses a neighborhood of q. Choose a real smooth function B on E2. Suppress the product pullback notation and set
α=∂A∧bar∂B+bar∂A∧∂B.
This is a real (1,1)-form, globally ambient-smooth on X, and zero on a neighborhood of its singular locus. It also has the expression
α=∂(A bar∂B)+bar∂(A∂B),
since the two A∂bar∂B terms cancel. Therefore dd^cα=0. It need not be d-closed. In fact
∂α=−∂A∧∂bar∂B+∂bar∂A∧∂B.
Choose a point r∈Creg at which ∂A(r)=0 and ∂bar∂A(r)≠0, and a point s∈E2 at which ∂B(s)≠0. Such functions are supplied by local quadratic and linear functions times cutoffs. Then ∂α(r,s)≠0. Thus dα≠0.

Write α~ for its smooth pullback to Y. Let K0=λκ1+κ2. Define the finite constants
rH=sup over Y\D of the operator norm of α~ relative to H0,
rK=sup over Y of the operator norm of α~ relative to K0.
The first is finite because α~ vanishes near D. For any nonzero ε with |ε|rH<1/2 and |ε|rK<1/2, set h=h0+εα on X and H=π*h=H0+εα~ on Y. Then h is a strictly positive ambient-smooth background. Near the cusp it equals h0; on the support of α it is an ordinary positive smooth surface metric, which also gives positive local ambient extensions. It is genuinely nonclosed because dh=εdα≠0 on Xreg. Upstairs H remains degenerate along D, and dd^cH=0.

4. Explicit repair, not a positivity assumption. The function λ−ρ has zero κ1-integral. On the flat torus E1, Fourier inversion of the mean-zero Laplacian produces a unique smooth real mean-zero v satisfying
dd^c v=(λ−ρ)κ1.
Concretely, each nonzero Fourier coefficient of v is the corresponding coefficient of λ−ρ divided by the nonzero negative eigenvalue of dd^c/κ1; smoothness follows from rapid decay. Set v0=pr1*v on Y. Then
k=H+dd^c v0=K0+εα~ ≥ K0/2.
Thus k is genuinely positive, smooth, pluriclosed, and nonclosed. The positivity was obtained by adding an explicit reference potential; it was not attributed to π*h.

5. Genuine disk descent. Every holomorphic disk into the cusp lifts holomorphically. If its components satisfy y^2=x^3 and x is not identically zero, set z=y/x off {x=0}. Then z^2=x, z^3=y, and |z|^2=|x|, so z extends holomorphically over the zeros by the removable-singularity theorem. If x is identically zero, so is y, and the lift is the constant disk. Together with the unchanged E2 component this lifts every disk into X to Y. Since π is a homeomorphism, any continuous U on Y has a unique continuous descended function u=U∘π^{-1}. If H+dd^cU≥0 for a C^2 U, lifted disks show exactly the required h-subharmonic disk condition downstairs: on a disk f, the chosen p_f has dd^cp_f=f*h, and dd^c(U∘f~+p_f)=f~*(H+dd^cU)≥0. In particular v0 descends to a bounded continuous genuine h-psh function. All values are finite canonical values. No assertion that an arbitrary smooth solution on an arbitrary resolution descends is being used.

A positive local-embedding form h_C with the stated local model is obtained by a smooth partition of unity, taking the ambient Euclidean form in the cusp chart and positive forms elsewhere. Near p its pullback is
δ(|z|⁴+|z|⁶)=(i/(2π))(4|z|²+9|z|⁴)dz∧dbar z.
It is smooth, positive off p, and zero only at p. Relative to κ_1 it is ρκ_1 with the asserted properties. Its average λ is strictly positive. On a curve a smooth (1,1)-form is closed, so H_0 is closed. Its ranks are as stated.

Choose A by a bump function supported in the regular locus, equal near r to a real function with a nonzero Hessian and zero first derivative; choose B with nonzero first derivative at s. Complex conjugation interchanges the two terms defining α, so α is real. Direct differentiation gives
α=∂(A bar∂B)+bar∂(A∂B),
∂bar∂α=0,
∂α=−∂A∧∂bar∂B+∂bar∂A∧∂B.
At (r,s) the last expression is nonzero. Thus dα≠0, whereas δα=0. Because A is supported away from q, α is ambient-smooth and vanishes near the singular locus.

The support of α upstairs is separated from D, where H_0 is the only degenerate form. On that support H_0 is uniformly positive. Consequently r_H is finite, and r_K is finite by compactness. The two operator-norm inequalities give H≥H_0/2 off D and k≥K_0/2. Near D, α=0, so H=H_0 and has rank one. Downstairs h is ambient-positive near the singular locus, and positive on the regular locus by the first inequality; a positive intrinsic form on a smooth embedding extends locally to a positive ambient form. Hence it has the required local-embedding positivity everywhere. Since h_0 is closed on the regular locus and dα≠0 there, dh≠0 for ε≠0. Also δH=0.

The equation δv=(λ−ρ)κ_1 has a unique smooth zero-mean solution. Indeed its right-hand coefficient has zero mean; on the flat elliptic curve invert the nonzero Fourier symbols of ∂²/(∂z∂bar z). Their quadratic growth and the rapid decay of the smooth right-hand side give a smooth solution. The only zero symbol is the constant mode. Pulling back v yields H+δv_0=K_0+εα, establishing the assertion concerning k.

For a disk in a cusp chart write its coordinates as x(t),y(t). If x is not identically zero, z=y/x is holomorphic away from its zeros and satisfies z²=x and z³=y. The bound |z|²=|x| makes all such singularities removable. If x is identically zero, y is identically zero, and the lift is constant p in that factor. Together with the unchanged second factor, this gives a unique holomorphic disk lift. Local lifts agree by injectivity of π.

A continuous U has a unique continuous descent because π is a homeomorphism. If U is C² and H+δU≥0, every lifted disk f̃ satisfies
δ(U∘f̃+p_f)=f̃*(H+δU)≥0.
Thus the descended function passes the specified genuine disk tests, with its continuous canonical values. This applies to U=v_0 since k>0. It is bounded and finite everywhere; no distributional derivative on a pole disk is involved.

notes.summary: Full two-complex-dimensional nonlinear existence for an open Sobolev family of measures on the cuspidal surface of n1, proved by Fourier/Neumann inversion and contraction, not a one-dimensional Green construction or a assumed Monge–Ampère existence theorem.
notes.detailedSummary: On Y, k=K0+εα~ is positive and dd^c-closed. For an integer s≥5, the linearization Lε w=2k∧dd^cw/K0^2 is an invertible small perturbation of a flat torus Laplacian on zero-mean H^{s+2}→H^s. The quadratic term Q(w)=(dd^cw)^2/K0^2 has zero mean and a Sobolev algebra Lipschitz bound. Explicit smallness constants give a contraction solving (k+dd^cw)^2=F K0^2 for every positive H^s density F sufficiently close to k^2/K0^2 with the same integral. For arbitrary positive f, normalize F=M f/∫fK0^2, M=∫k^2. The downstairs datum is ν=π_*(fK0^2), the equation constant is c=M/ν(X), and u=(v0+w)∘π^{-1}−sup descends genuinely and continuously. notes.text:
NONLINEAR SOLVABILITY WITH EXPLICIT SMALLNESS. Use the geometric construction in n1. Everything below takes place on the real four-dimensional flat torus Y=E1×E2. Write Ω=K0^2 (no factorial in this convention), α for α~, k=K0+εα, and
M=∫Y k^2>0, fε=k^2/Ω.
The positivity estimates of n1 imply fε≥1/4.

Fix an integer s≥5. Use Fourier Sobolev norms on the torus. Let H^s_0 denote real functions with zero Ω-integral. Define
L0w=2K0∧dd^cw/Ω,
Lαw=2α∧dd^cw/Ω,
Lε=L0+εLα.
The operator L0 is a constant-coefficient Laplacian, with the normalization inherited from dd^c=(i/(2π))∂bar∂. On every nonzero Fourier mode its eigenvalue is negative and its magnitude is comparable to |m|^2. Consequently Fourier division proves that L0:H^{s+2}_0→H^s_0 has bounded inverse. Denote its norm by A0. Multiplication by the fixed smooth coefficients of α gives a finite operator bound B_s=||Lα||_{H^{s+2}→H^s}. The zero-mean property of Lα follows, with no closedness assumption on α beyond dd^cα=0, from
∫Y Lαw Ω=2∫Y dd^cw∧α=2∫Y w dd^cα=0.

Impose the additional explicit geometric smallness condition |ε|A0B_s≤1/2. It is compatible with all conditions of n1 and ε≠0. Neumann inversion of I+εL0^{-1}Lα proves that Lε:H^{s+2}_0→H^s_0 is invertible, with inverse norm A≤2A0. This is an independently proved solvability statement, not a hypothesis asserting that a nonlinear equation already has a solution.

Set Q(w)=(dd^cw)^2/Ω. Since real dimension is four and s>2, H^s is an algebra. The algebra estimate can be obtained directly from Fourier convolution, using the ℓ^1 bound on Fourier coefficients furnished by ∑m(1+|m|^2)^{−s}<∞. Thus there is a computable finite C_s, depending only on the fixed torus and s, such that
||Q(w)||_{H^s}≤C_s||w||_{H^{s+2}}^2,
||Q(w)−Q(z)||_{H^s}≤C_s(||w||_{H^{s+2}}+||z||_{H^{s+2}})||w−z||_{H^{s+2}}.
Also ∫YQ(w)Ω=∫Y(dd^cw)^2=0, by Stokes. These identities are first proved for Fourier polynomials and then extended by Sobolev approximation.

Let D_s be a Fourier Sobolev bound for the K0-operator norm of dd^cw:
||dd^cw||_{L∞,K0}≤D_s||w||_{H^{s+2}}.
It is finite by Cauchy–Schwarz on the Fourier series (s>2 suffices). Choose
0<R≤min{1/(4AC_s),1/(4D_s)}, and δ=R/(2A).
For any g∈H^s_0 with ||g||_{H^s}≤δ, the map
T(w)=Lε^{-1}(g−Q(w))
is a contraction of the closed radius-R ball in H^{s+2}_0 into itself. Indeed its image norm is at most Aδ+AC_sR^2≤3R/4, and its Lipschitz constant is at most 2AC_sR≤1/2. Banach contraction, or its elementary successive-approximation proof, gives w∈H^{s+2}_0 with
Lεw+Q(w)=g.
The Hessian bound ensures
k+dd^cw ≥ K0/2−K0/4=K0/4.
Since H^{s+2} embeds into C^2 (in fact much better for s≥5), the resulting equation holds as an equality of continuous densities and ordinary positive top-degree forms. The solution is a genuine potential under the disk definition.

MEASURE HYPOTHESES AND NORMALIZATION. Let f be a strictly positive real H^s function on Y; no restriction that it depend on only one factor is made. Define
ν=π_*(fΩ), c=M/(∫Y fΩ), F=cf.
Assume the explicit, scaling-invariant condition
||F−fε||_{H^s}≤δ.
Then g=F−fε has zero mean, so the construction gives
(k+dd^cw)^2=FΩ.
Set U=v0+w and let u=U∘π^{-1}−sup_Y U. Constants do not affect the equation. By n1, u descends continuously with all canonical disk values, and
MA_ext,h(u)=π_*((H+dd^cU)^2)=π_*(FΩ)=cν.
The normalization is exactly sup_Xu=0. The measure has finite mass, since f is continuous on compact Y. Its non-pluripolar property follows from the standard local fact that smooth volume does not charge pluripolar sets and from pulling a local defining psh function back through the finite normalization. The inverse image of the singular locus is the smooth divisor D, which has Ω-measure zero.

This is not a one-dimensional linear construction in disguise. The one-dimensional Fourier primitive v0 only repairs the reference background. Actual prescribed densities form an open neighborhood, after mass normalization, in the full H^s space of functions of four real variables; the equation contains the genuinely quadratic term (dd^cw)^2. For an explicit nontrivial example, choose periodic real coordinates on the two elliptic factors and take a nonzero small multiple of g=cos(2πx1)cos(2πx2)+cos(2πy1)cos(2πy2). It has zero mean. The density f=fε+t g is positive and meets the condition for small |t|>0, with c=1, and contraction produces a nonconstant solution without prescribing it in advance.

CONTINUITY MODULUS. U is C^1 on Y, so it is locally Lipschitz. The cusp normalization inverse is locally Hölder with exponent 1/3 in ambient coordinates. To check this for arbitrary pairs z,z', put d=z−z', a=z+z'. Then
z^2−z'^2=da,
z^3−z'^3=d(3a^2+d^2)/4.
If |a|≥|d|/4, the first expression has magnitude at least |d|^2/4, which controls |d|^3 on a bounded small chart. If |a|<|d|/4, the second expression has magnitude at least 13|d|^3/64. Thus
|z−z'|≤C(|z^2−z'^2|+|z^3−z'^3|)^{1/3}.
Combining this with the ordinary elliptic-coordinate component proves that the full potential u, not a residual after subtracting a pole, is locally Hölder 1/3 downstairs in local embedding coordinates. There are no poles in this package. On Xreg it has the Sobolev and C^2 regularity inherited from U via a biholomorphic chart.

reconstruction.statement:
Use the geometry and forms X,Y,π,h,H,v_0,k,K_0,α̃ and nonzero ε of w7-1/n1, and write α=α̃ upstairs. Let Ω=K_0^2, with no divided-volume factorial, M=∫_Y k^2>0, and f_ε=k^2/Ω≥1/4. Fix an integer s≥5, use Fourier Sobolev norms on the real four-dimensional torus Y, and let H^s_0 denote real functions of zero Ω-mean. Define L_0w=2K_0∧δw/Ω, L_αw=2α∧δw/Ω, and L_ε=L_0+εL_α, where δ=(i/(2π))∂bar∂. The operator L_0:H^{s+2}_0→H^s_0 is invertible. Let A_0=||L_0^{−1}|| and B_s=||L_α||_{H^{s+2}→H^s}<∞. The operator L_α has zero Ω-integral on every input. If |ε|A_0B_s≤1/2, then L_ε:H^{s+2}_0→H^s_0 is invertible with inverse norm A≤2A_0.
For Q(w)=(δw)^2/Ω there is a finite constant C_s, depending only on the fixed torus and s, such that ||Q(w)||_{H^s}≤C_s||w||_{H^{s+2}}^2 and ||Q(w)−Q(z)||_{H^s}≤C_s(||w||_{H^{s+2}}+||z||_{H^{s+2}})||w−z||_{H^{s+2}}. Every Q(w) has zero Ω-integral. There is a finite D_s such that ||δw||_{L∞,K_0}≤D_s||w||_{H^{s+2}}. Choose 0<R≤min{(4AC_s)^{−1},(4D_s)^{−1}} and δ_0=R/(2A). For every g∈H^s_0 with ||g||_{H^s}≤δ_0, there exists w∈H^{s+2}_0 with ||w||_{H^{s+2}}≤R satisfying L_εw+Q(w)=g, equivalently (k+δw)^2=(f_ε+g)Ω, and k+δw≥K_0/4. This solution is C^2 and the equation is an equality of continuous densities.
Let f∈H^s(Y) be real and strictly positive, define ν=π_*(fΩ), c=M/∫_Y fΩ, and F=cf, and assume ||F−f_ε||_{H^s}≤δ_0. Then there is a w as above with g=F−f_ε. For U=v_0+w, the function u=U∘π^{−1}−sup_Y U is finite, continuous, genuine canonical h-plurisubharmonic, and satisfies MA_ext,h(u)=π_*((H+δU)^2)=cν and sup_Xu=0. The datum ν is finite, positive, and non-pluripolar, and ν({q}×E_2)=0. All forms and equations use δ=(i/(2π))∂bar∂ without a divided-volume factorial. The condition on f is invariant under multiplying f by a positive constant and permits full four-real-variable perturbations, without a separability requirement.
The full potential u, not a residual, is locally Hölder of exponent 1/3 in local embedding coordinates downstairs and is at least C^2 on X_reg, with the regularity inherited from U∈H^{s+2}(Y). There are no poles. On a bounded small cusp chart, for all z,z′, |z−z′|≤C(|z^2−z′^2|+|z^3−z′^3|)^{1/3}.
In periodic real coordinates z_j=x_j+iy_j, the mean-zero function G=cos(2πx_1)cos(2πx_2)+cos(2πy_1)cos(2πy_2) gives nontrivial prescribed data: for every sufficiently small nonzero real t, f=f_ε+tG is positive and satisfies the stated norm bound, c=1, and the resulting correction w is nonconstant.
reconstruction.proof:
We use only the geometry of w7-1/n1. All norms below are the fixed Fourier Sobolev norms on the four-real-dimensional torus. Fourier inversion proves that L_0 is an isomorphism on zero-mean functions: its nonconstant symbols are negative definite quadratic functions of the frequency. The supremum of (1+|m|²) divided by their absolute values is finite and is its H^s-to-H^{s+2} inverse bound A_0.

For smooth w, integration by parts gives ∫α∧δw=∫w δα=0. Smooth multiplication and differentiation are bounded in the indicated Sobolev spaces, so L_α is bounded and has zero integral for all H^{s+2} inputs by density. The same holds for L_0. The inequality |ε|A_0B_s≤1/2 allows inversion of I+εL_0^−1L_α by its geometric series on H^{s+2}_0; the inverse norm of L_ε is at most 2A_0.

Here are the estimates used in the nonlinear step. For s>2, Cauchy–Schwarz on Fourier coefficients gives H^s⊂C^0 and weighted convolution gives ||ab||_{H^s}≤C||a||_{H^s}||b||_{H^s}. Applying this to the finitely many second derivatives in Q gives its quadratic bound and, by factoring Q(w)−Q(z), its stated Lipschitz bound. Smooth coefficient multipliers are bounded by the same argument. The Fourier embedding applied to second derivatives gives D_s. Stokes gives ∫(δw)²=0 for smooth w, because (δw)²=δ(wδw); density and the product estimate extend this identity to H^{s+2}. Thus Q takes values in H^s_0.

On the closed radius-R ball define T(w)=L_ε^−1(g−Q(w)). Its norm is at most R/2+AC_sR²≤3R/4, and its Lipschitz constant is at most 2AC_sR≤1/2. Iteration converges in the complete Sobolev space to a fixed point. The expansion of (k+δw)² proves the stated equation. Moreover ||δw||_{L∞,K_0}≤1/4, so k+δw≥K_0/4. Fourier summability gives H^{s+2}⊂C² for the specified s, so these are pointwise inequalities and the density is continuous.

For the datum f, c∫fΩ=M and ∫f_εΩ=M show that g=cf−f_ε has zero mean. The size hypothesis permits the preceding construction. For U=v_0+w, H+δU=k+δw, so the homeomorphism and disk-lifting argument of w7-1/n1 give a finite continuous genuine h-plurisubharmonic descent. Constants leave its Hessian unchanged. Its extended measure, calculated on this resolution, is precisely π*((k+δw)²)=cπ*(fΩ). The normalization is therefore correct, with no factorial adjustment.

The smooth-volume measure fΩ is finite and assigns zero mass to D. If a local pluripolar Borel set downstairs is contained in the poles of a nontrivial genuine local plurisubharmonic function, its pullback is contained in the poles of a nontrivial plurisubharmonic function upstairs. Nontriviality is preserved by surjectivity and connected local neighborhoods; plurisubharmonicity follows from disk lifting and the smooth-space disk criterion. Such a function is locally integrable and its pole set has Lebesgue measure zero. Hence ν is non-pluripolar and gives zero mass to the singular divisor.

To check the quantitative descent, put d=|z−z′| and a=|z+z′|. If a≥d/2, |z²−z′²|=da≥d²/2, which controls d³ on a bounded chart. If a<d/2, then
|z²+zz′+z′²|=|3(z+z′)²+(z−z′)²|/4≥d²/16,
so |z³−z′³|≥d³/16. This proves the displayed inverse Hölder estimate. Since U is C² and therefore locally Lipschitz upstairs, it descends with exponent 1/3 in the cusp-product embedding. Away from the divisor π is biholomorphic, giving the stated C² regularity. It is the full finite potential; there are no poles.

Finally G has zero mean, is smooth and nonzero. For small nonzero t, f_ε+tG is strictly positive and satisfies the norm bound; its integral is M, so c=1. A constant correction would give Q(w)=L_εw=0, contrary to g=tG. This supplies genuinely nonconstant, nonseparable perturbations.

notes.summary: Mass conservation and constant-difference uniqueness in the entire bounded canonical type for the pluriclosed surface construction. The key energy identity uses dd^c of the sum of the two metric currents, not d-closedness. A torus convolution proof reduces all rough-potential limits to the foundational weighted Bedford–Taylor decreasing convergence theorem; its exact primary-source audit is still outstanding.
notes.detailedSummary: For bounded k-psh U on a compact surface with dd^ck=0, bounded BT calculus gives ∫(k+dd^cU)^2=∫k^2. If V is the C^2 strictly positive solution from n2 and U is any bounded canonical k-psh solution with the same measure, convolve U,V,k on the flat torus. The convolved positive forms A_j,B_j satisfy dd^c(A_j+B_j)=0 and B_j≥βK0. Consequently −∫(U_j−V_j)(A_j^2−B_j^2)=∫d(U_j−V_j)∧d^c(U_j−V_j)∧(A_j+B_j)≥β times the flat Dirichlet energy. Local bounded weighted BT monotone convergence makes the left side tend to zero. Poincaré then implies U−V is constant. This covers all bounded potentials, not merely smooth ones. The remaining external foundational input is specifically the weighted decreasing BT convergence and no-pluripolar-mass statements; source metadata is supplied, but not a completed literal primary-text check.
notes.text:
ROUGH UNIQUENESS AND FINITE MASS. This note isolates the only foundational pluripotential input not independently reconstructed here. Input BT: on a coordinate ball, locally uniformly bounded decreasing sequences of plurisubharmonic functions have decreasing-limit Bedford–Taylor products; the associated bounded psh weighted mixed products also converge. These bounded products do not charge pluripolar sets. Relevant primary sources are E. Bedford and B. A. Taylor, The Dirichlet problem for a complex Monge–Ampère equation, Invent. Math. 37 (1976), 1–44, and A new capacity for plurisubharmonic functions, Acta Math. 149 (1982), 1–40. No theorem number or literal-text verification is claimed in this invocation. In particular the weighted version, not merely unweighted weak convergence, must be checked against the primary text or reconstructed. All uses and hypotheses of that input are made explicit below.

1. Class and products. On Y, k is the positive smooth metric of n1 with dd^ck=0. A bounded canonical k-psh function W satisfies k+dd^cW≥0. On each coordinate ball choose a smooth strictly psh quadratic q with dd^cq≥k. Then W+q is locally bounded psh. Thus its non-pluripolar square is the ordinary bounded BT square, and the square of k+dd^cW is defined by expanding relative to the positive closed current dd^c(W+q) and the smooth form k−dd^cq. This expansion is independent of q. Input BT shows that it does not charge local pluripolar sets.

2. Mass formula. Write A=k+dd^cW. In the sense of bounded BT products,
A^2=k^2+2k∧dd^cW+(dd^cW)^2.
On the compact torus,
∫k∧dd^cW=∫W dd^ck=0,
∫(dd^cW)^2=0.
The last is the compact Stokes identity for the globally defined BT current dd^c(W dd^cW); equivalently use the decreasing regularizations described below and their weak convergence. Therefore
∫Y A^2=∫Y k^2=M.
This also proves finite mass for every bounded potential in the entire type, not just for the constructed solution. For H=k−dd^cv0 the same conclusion holds, either by replacing W by W−v0 or directly using dd^cH=0. For any claimed equation A^2=c fΩ with f positive, c is necessarily M/∫fΩ.

3. Convolution with positivity retained. Let U be any bounded canonical k-psh function, and let V be the C^2 solution from n2; B=k+dd^cV≥βK0 for β=1/4. Convolve globally on the flat torus with a nonnegative small radial kernel ρ_j supported in a coordinate ball of radius r_j↓0. Put
U_j=U*ρ_j, V_j=V*ρ_j, k_j=k*ρ_j,
A_j=k_j+dd^cU_j, B_j=k_j+dd^cV_j.
Translation and convolution preserve positivity, so A_j≥0 and B_j≥βK0. Also dd^ck_j=0, and k_j→k smoothly. The smooth V_j converge in C^2 to V.

For the BT limit hypotheses, choose a constant C so dd^cU≥−C times a flat positive form, and similarly for V. On small coordinate balls, U plus a fixed positive quadratic is psh. Radial averages of a subharmonic function decrease as the averaging radius decreases. Thus there is a fixed b≥0 such that U_j+b r_j^2 decreases to the canonical U; the same b can be taken for V. The added constants do not affect dd^c or the differences U_j−V_j. Locally, after adding a fixed quadratic, these are uniformly bounded decreasing psh sequences, precisely the hypotheses of Input BT.

4. Smooth identity that removes the apparent torsion problem. Set φ_j=U_j−V_j and T_j=A_j+B_j. Then
A_j^2−B_j^2=dd^cφ_j∧T_j,
dd^cT_j=0.
For a real smooth φ,
dd^c(φ^2)=2φ dd^cφ+2dφ∧d^cφ.
Integrating this against T_j and using compact Stokes gives
−∫Y φ_j(A_j^2−B_j^2)=∫Y dφ_j∧d^cφ_j∧T_j.
The right side is nonnegative and at least
β∫Y dφ_j∧d^cφ_j∧K0.
This identity requires dd^cT_j=0, not dT_j=0. In particular it is valid for the genuinely nonclosed background; no unaccounted torsion term was discarded.

5. Justification of the rough limit. Suppose A^2=B^2 as measures. Expand A_j relative to the positive closed current P_j=C Kflat+dd^cU_j and the smoothly converging coefficient form k_j−C Kflat. Input BT gives convergence of the unweighted square and all terms weighted by U_j; V_j converges uniformly and is smooth in the limit. In detail, the four terms in
∫φ_j(A_j^2−B_j^2)
are ∫U_j A_j^2, −∫V_j A_j^2, −∫U_j B_j^2, and ∫V_j B_j^2. The first uses weighted decreasing BT convergence after the quadratic shifts; the second uses unweighted BT convergence and uniform convergence of V_j; the third uses ordinary dominated convergence against smoothly converging densities; the fourth is smooth convergence. The constants b r_j^2 vanish. Consequently the left side of the smooth identity tends to
−∫Y (U−V)(A^2−B^2)=0.
This proves that the flat Dirichlet energy of φ_j tends to zero. Boundedness and canonical convergence give φ_j→U−V in L^2. Fourier Poincaré on the torus then shows U−V is constant. This establishes uniqueness against every bounded canonical potential, not just against a regular competitor. If the constants c in two equations were initially different, the mass formula first makes them equal.

6. Relation to the downstairs singularity class. Ordinary type of zero on X is exactly all bounded genuine h-psh functions: both inequalities with the reference zero forbid poles and give a uniform two-sided bound. A member of this type pulls back to a bounded genuine H-psh function on Y, by composition of disk tests. Positivity of its current on the smooth torus follows locally by adding a dominating quadratic. Conversely the constructed solution descends by the explicit disk lifting in n1. Subtracting v0 reduces its upstairs equation to the k-background equation just proved. Since π is a homeomorphism, an upstairs constant difference is a downstairs constant difference with the same canonical values.

7. Refinements. For a modification μ:Z→Y, bounded canonical pullbacks have bounded local psh shifts, and hence by Input BT their products do not charge the analytic exceptional locus. On its complement μ is biholomorphic and the products agree by local change of coordinates. Therefore
μ_* MA_{μ*H}(W∘μ)=MA_H(W).
In particular one must not call μ*H or μ*k strictly positive; either may degenerate. Any smooth resolution of this particular X factors through Y. Locally this can be seen directly: pull back x,y with y^2=x^3, and extend z=y/x holomorphically from the dense regular preimage using |z|^2=|x| and normality of the smooth source. This gives a holomorphic lift to the cusp normalization, and the lifts glue. The factor is a proper birational modification of Y. Thus all common refinements give the same downstairs measure. For the constructed U, its further pullback is literally U∘μ, constant on every compact μ-fiber with its finite canonical value. There is no unproved descent step on a refinement.

Remaining verification: the weighted decreasing convergence and non-pluripolar-mass facts in Input BT have not been checked literally against the primary papers in this invocation. All nonlinear solvability, geometry, energy identities, and normalization are proved independently; resolving that foundational source audit would close the corresponding verification requirement in the problem.

We use the listed bounded recursive, mixed decreasing, weighted decreasing and non-pluripolarity premises, retaining locally bounded canonical representatives throughout.

First record the local calculus. Write P=W+q, with q smooth strictly plurisubharmonic and δq≥k on a smaller coordinate ball. Then P is bounded plurisubharmonic and
A²=(δP)²+2(k−δq)∧δP+(k−δq)².
The recursive mixed calculus and multilinearity show that changing q gives the same expansion. Each nonsmooth term has zero mass on pluripolar sets: locally its total variation is bounded by a constant times the corresponding positive product wedged with the flat form to complementary degree, to which the stated non-pluripolarity premise applies. The smooth term has the same property. For locally bounded potentials the local truncations used in non-pluripolar products are eventually stationary on smaller balls. Thus the bounded expansion is the extended product. Positivity can also be checked by simultaneous convolution, as described next.

A bounded quasi-plurisubharmonic function W on the flat torus has δW≥−C K_0. Let W_r be convolution with a fixed nonnegative radial kernel of radius r. On a coordinate ball choose a fixed quadratic q with δq=C K_0. Then
(W+q)*ρ_r=W_r+q+b r²
for a fixed b≥0. Spherical means of a subharmonic function increase with radius; integrating these means against the radial kernel shows that W_{r_j}+q+b r_j² decreases to the canonical W+q when r_j decreases to zero. The sequences are locally uniformly bounded. If k_j=k*ρ_{r_j}, then A_j=k_j+δW_{r_j} is positive, being convolution of the positive current A. Expand A_j relative to the Hessian of the preceding plurisubharmonic shift. Mixed decreasing continuity and smooth coefficient convergence give A_j²→A²; in particular A² is positive. Weighted decreasing continuity gives W_{r_j}A_j²→WA² after subtracting q+b r_j² from the weight. These statements also hold with another bounded quasi-plurisubharmonic weight or with mixed products of separately regularized potentials; all shifted sequences meet the same local boundedness and monotonicity hypotheses.

For mass, the recursive identity extends to bounded quasi-plurisubharmonic functions by writing W=P−q and expanding:
(δW)²=δ(WδW).
Here WδW is canonical multiplication of an order-zero signed current. The terms involving smooth q cancel using δ(qδP)=δq∧δP and the defining recursion for P. On the compact torus Stokes and distributional integration by parts give
∫(δW)²=0,  ∫k∧δW=∫Wδk=0.
Consequently ∫A²=∫k²=M. The same argument applies to H, since δH=0. Applying it to the smooth v_0 in k=H+δv_0 proves ∫H²=M. Finiteness also follows directly from the local order-zero expansions and a finite cover.

We now prove uniqueness against every bounded competitor. Put t=U−V, A=k+δU, B=k+δV. Convolve both potentials and k simultaneously, obtaining t_j, A_j, B_j. They are smooth, A_j≥0 and B_j≥βK_0. Also δk_j=0, hence δ(A_j+B_j)=0. The smooth identity δ(t_j²)=2t_jδt_j+2dt_j∧d^ct_j and Stokes yield
∫t_j(A_j²−B_j²)=∫t_jδt_j∧(A_j+B_j)
=−∫dt_j∧d^ct_j∧(A_j+B_j).
The weighted convergence established above, applied separately to the U_j and V_j weights and all expanded products, makes the left side converge to ∫t(A²−B²)=0. The right-hand energy is nonnegative after changing sign, and bounds below β∫dt_j∧d^ct_j∧K_0. The latter is a fixed positive multiple of a uniformly elliptic L² gradient norm. Thus ||∇t_j||_2→0. Convolution preserves the mean, and Fourier Poincaré implies t_j converges in L² to its constant mean. Since it also converges to t in L², t is constant almost everywhere. Canonical quasi-plurisubharmonic representatives are determined by their almost-everywhere values: locally shift by q and recover each value by shrinking ball means. Hence U−V is constant at every point, not just almost everywhere.

The supplied inspection w87-1/n2 identifies Bedford–Taylor, A new capacity for plurisubharmonic functions, Acta Math. 149 (1982), 1–40. Printed p.4, equation (2.1), defines mixed currents recursively as distributions. Theorem 2.1 on p.4 gives weak convergence of mixed products when each locally bounded psh input decreases everywhere to its locally bounded psh limit. Theorem 2.4, printed p.7 with the top-degree argument on pp.8–9, also supplies psh-weighted decreasing convergence, but below that additional statement is reconstructed rather than needed as an independent input.

Recursion, symmetry, positivity, and weak convergence are unaffected by this fixed positive factor. For a smooth function in complex dimension d,
(δu)^d=d!π^{-d}det(u_{j bar k}) dλ,

The defining recursion gives μ∧δv=δ(vμ). Since μ has top base degree, every differentiation term involving a z differential vanishes. Thus only the vertical δ_w remains. For every real t,
δ_w max(t,log|w|²)
is unit uniform circle mass at |w|=exp(t/2). Indeed the Euclidean Laplacian has mass 4π at that circle, from the outward derivative jump 0 to 2/|w|, and δ_w equals (1/(4π)) times the Laplacian measure. This also directly verifies the normalization used here.

The equality as currents remains valid for bounded Borel canonical a: test δ(vμ), apply Fubini in w, and use the preceding one-variable distribution identity. It does not require μ to avoid the discontinuities of a. Hence μ∧δv is precisely the measure obtained by integrating these probability circles against μ(z).

Choose a smooth compactly supported radial test θ(w) in the annulus r<|w|<R that equals log|w|² near all circles with radii exp(t/2), L≤t≤U. For every smooth compactly supported ξ(z),
⟨μ_j∧δv_j,ξθ⟩=∫ξa_j dμ_j,
⟨μ∧δv,ξθ⟩=∫ξa dμ.
Unweighted convergence proves the claim. Lower-degree weighted currents follow by wedging with fixed flat quadratic potentials, then polarization of the constant positive test forms. Subtracting a fixed smooth quadratic proves the same result for quasi-psh weights with a common lower Hessian bound. Smoothly varying coefficient forms are allowed because they converge uniformly on compact sets and the positive mixed currents have uniformly bounded local masses. This is the weighted limit used in n2; it agrees with, but does not have to assume, the source's Theorem 2.4.

3. Why the torus regularizations meet the hypotheses.

On a flat torus let W be bounded canonical quasi-psh with δW≥−Cω_flat. Convolve with a nonnegative radial kernel ρ_r, obtained by scaling one fixed kernel, and write W_r=W*ρ_r. On a coordinate ball choose the fixed positive quadratic q with δq=Cω_flat. There is a fixed b≥0 for which
(W+q)*ρ_r=W_r+q+br².
A radial average is a positive mixture of spherical averages. Spherical averages of the real subharmonic function W+q are nondecreasing with radius. Consequently W_{r_j}+q+br_j² decreases everywhere to W+q as r_j↓0. The canonical mean-value/upper-semicontinuity properties identify the limit with the genuine representative, not a null-set modification. These are locally uniformly bounded psh sequences.

If a smooth nonclosed background K is convolved simultaneously, K_j→K smoothly. Expanding (K_j+δW_j)^r relative to the closed positive current δ(W_j+q+br_j²) puts every unweighted or W_j-weighted term within the preceding BT hypotheses. One does not apply a closed-current BT theorem directly to the nonclosed positive current K_j+δW_j.

On a coordinate ball any bounded quasi-psh W has a bounded psh shift W+q. The powers of δW and of K+δW are defined by the finite expansions relative to δ(W+q) and smooth coefficient forms. Symmetry and the recursive definition make these expansions independent of q. In particular
(δW)^r=δ(W(δW)^{r−1})
as currents, for the bounded canonical representative. The product with W is the bounded weighted product furnished by the same recursion/expansion.

The non-pluripolar truncations of a bounded local psh shift are stationary for all sufficiently large truncation indices. Thus in this bounded situation the extended product in the task agrees with this bounded product. For exceptional-set/refinement arguments below, we use the stipulated non-pluripolar nature and modification locality of the extended products. A separate application of the 1982 capacity theorem is therefore unnecessary. Data non-pluripolarity will be proved directly from smooth-volume nullity of the poles of a nontrivial local psh function.

This closes the mathematical foundational gap isolated in the earlier construction: the actual external inputs are bounded recursion and ordinary mixed decreasing continuity, with their primary statements and normalization now identified. No general Hermitian Monge–Ampère existence or log-terminal continuity theorem is used.

For every r_j↓0, the functions W_{r_j}+q+br_j^2 form a locally uniformly bounded decreasing plurisubharmonic sequence with limit the genuine canonical W+q.

The normalization and smooth determinant computation follow from w87-1/n1: D=4πδ, so each differentiated factor contributes (4π)^−1 when replacing D by δ. Multiplication by a weight, whenever defined, leaves this scalar unchanged. The smooth top-degree formula is d!π^−d det(u_{j bar k})dλ.

For the weighted statement one can directly apply w87-1/n2, whose hypotheses are satisfied: all sequences decrease to locally bounded canonical plurisubharmonic limits and are bounded on each compact set between their limits and first terms. Its Theorem 2.4 premise includes all degrees r and independent weight sequences. Equivalently the derivation in w7-1/n5 proves the same assertion from ordinary decreasing continuity. A quasi-plurisubharmonic weight with a common lower Hessian bound is shifted by one smooth quadratic, and the quadratic contribution is subtracted using ordinary convergence. Positive-current trace bounds give uniformly bounded local coefficient variations. Hence multiplying by locally uniformly convergent smooth coefficient forms is legitimate, proving the assertion for every coefficient, not just traces.

For torus convolution, work on a ball larger than the compact testing set and take radii smaller than its margin. With q a fixed quadratic satisfying δq=Cω_flat, radial symmetry gives
q*ρ_r=q+b r²,
where b=∫q(ξ)ρ_1(ξ) after dropping constant and linear terms; b≥0. Therefore (W+q)*ρ_r=W_r+q+b r². Radial convolution is an average of spherical means with radii proportional to r. Spherical means of a plurisubharmonic, hence subharmonic, function increase with radius. Thus these functions decrease as r_j decreases. Their limit is the canonical W+q, by the mean characterization of the genuine upper value. Local boundedness follows from boundedness of W+q on a larger ball. Their Hessians are δW_{r_j}+δq.

Put K_j=K*ρ_{r_j}. These forms converge to K in every smooth norm. Expand
(K_j+δW_{r_j})^r
relative to δ(W_{r_j}+q+b r_j²) and the smooth form K_j−δq. Mixed decreasing continuity proves convergence of every term. For the weighted expression use W_{r_j}=(W_{r_j}+q+b r_j²)−q−b r_j² and apply the weighted result termwise. The last scalar tends to zero, and local variation bounds control it. Fixed or smoothly converging coefficient forms can be included by the same bounds. If K+δW≥0, its convolution K_j+δW_{r_j} is positive because convolution averages translations of a positive current; no closedness is used.

Lastly consider the intrinsic local calculus. Write P=W+q and expand δW=δP−δq. The recursive mixed calculus, symmetry and multilinearity show independence of q. For every r, the current (δW)^{r−1} is closed. Expanding the defining recursion for P and using δ(qT)=δq∧T for a closed current T gives
δ(W(δW)^{r−1})=(δW)^r.
This can also be verified by binomial expansion: apply δ to each P-weighted mixed product by the defining recursion, and each q-weighted term by smooth multiplication; all intermediate terms cancel. Every multiplication is by the prescribed bounded representative, and the local definitions agree on overlaps. The identity consequently holds globally. Expanding powers of K+δW adds only smooth coefficient factors and preserves independence of q.

When K+δW is positive, simultaneous convolution shows positivity of its bounded products. On each smaller coordinate ball the plurisubharmonic shift P is bounded below, so its non-pluripolar truncations and indicators are eventually equal to P and 1 there. Therefore the extended products agree with these bounded products. This uses boundedness, not a continuity hypothesis for W.

notes.text:
HIGHER-DIMENSIONAL TORSION-RANK-TWO PACKAGE.

This is a genuine extension, not just a restatement of the surface construction. It produces examples and sufficient conditions in every complex dimension n≥2, while preserving uniqueness in the entire bounded canonical type. Use the cusp curve C, elliptic E1 and functions A,B of n1, and fix further elliptic curves E2,…,En with flat positive forms κ2,…,κn. Let
X=C×E2×…×En, Y=E1×…×En, π=π1×id.
The normalization π remains finite birational, degree one, bijective, and a homeomorphism. Its singular locus is {q}×E2×…×En, and its inverse image D is {p}×E2×…×En. Every disk lifts by the same explicit cusp formula as n1. All spaces are compact, connected, reduced and locally irreducible, with pure dimension n.

GEOMETRY AND TORSION. Let
h0=hC+Σ_{j=2}^nκj,
α=∂A∧bar∂B+bar∂A∧∂B,
h=h0+εα.
Here α is pulled back only from C×E2 and vanishes near the singular locus. Nonzero ε satisfying the relative-metric bounds of n1 makes h positive in the local-embedding sense and genuinely nonclosed. Upstairs
H=π*h=η+Σ_{j=2}^nκj+εα~
is smooth but has rank n−1 along D. The explicit first-factor Fourier function v0 repairs it to
k=H+dd^cv0=K0+εα~,
K0=λκ1+Σ_{j=2}^nκj.
Require |ε| times the relative operator norms of α with respect to H0 and K0 to be <1/2. The first norm is finite because α vanishes near D. Thus k≥K0/2, while H remains degenerate.

The extra structure responsible for arbitrary-dimensional rough uniqueness is
 dd^ck=0, dk∧d^ck=0,
and likewise for H. Indeed dk and d^ck are pulled back from the smooth complex surface E1×E2. They are 3-forms there; their wedge has degree six on a real four-dimensional source and is identically zero. The Leibniz formula consequently gives
 dd^c(k^r)=0 and dd^c(H^r)=0 for every r≥0.
This conclusion would be false for a generic pluriclosed metric in dimension at least three; the torsion-rank-two hypothesis is decisive.

FULL n-DIMENSIONAL SOLVABILITY. Put Ω=K0^n, M=∫Yk^n>0, and fε=k^n/Ω. Choose an integer s≥n+3. Let H^s_0 be the real Fourier Sobolev space of functions with zero Ω-integral. Define
Lεw=n k^{n−1}∧dd^cw/Ω,
L0w=n K0^{n−1}∧dd^cw/Ω.
L0 is a flat constant-coefficient Laplacian and has bounded inverse H^s_0→H^{s+2}_0 by Fourier division. Denote the inverse norm by A0. Since dd^c(k^{n−1})=0, ∫LεwΩ=0. The coefficient difference k^{n−1}−K0^{n−1} is a polynomial in ε with zero constant term. Therefore, on a fixed small ε interval allowed by positivity, there is a finite explicit coefficient bound
||Lε−L0||_{H^{s+2}→H^s}≤|ε|B_{n,s}.
It can be estimated by Sobolev multiplication norms of the fixed coefficients K0 and α~. Choose the additional geometric bound |ε|A0B_{n,s}≤1/2. Neumann inversion then gives ||Lε^{-1}||≤A=2A0.

Write
Qε(w)=Σ_{r=2}^n binom(n,r) k^{n−r}∧(dd^cw)^r/Ω.
Since s>n (real dimension is 2n), H^s is an algebra, proved by the same Fourier convolution estimate as n2. On the unit ball of H^{s+2}, the finite polynomial Qε satisfies
||Qε(w)||_{H^s}≤C_{n,s}||w||_{H^{s+2}}^2,
||Qε(w)−Qε(z)||_{H^s}≤C_{n,s}(||w||_{H^{s+2}}+||z||_{H^{s+2}})||w−z||_{H^{s+2}}.
There is no hidden mean obstruction: each term has zero integral, since compact integration by parts gives
∫k^{n−r}∧(dd^cw)^r=∫w dd^c(k^{n−r})∧(dd^cw)^{r−1}=0.
The computation is first performed on Fourier polynomials, then extended by Sobolev continuity.

Let D_{n,s} bound ||dd^cw||_{L∞,K0} by D_{n,s}||w||_{H^{s+2}}. It is finite by Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz since s>n. Choose
R≤min{1,1/(4AC_{n,s}),1/(4D_{n,s})}, δ=R/(2A).
For g∈H^s_0 with ||g||≤δ, the map w↦Lε^{-1}(g−Qε(w)) is a contraction on the radius-R ball. Its fixed point satisfies
(k+dd^cw)^n=(fε+g)Ω,
k+dd^cw≥K0/4.
This proof treats the full degree-n Monge–Ampère polynomial and unrestricted functions of n complex variables. It is not a one-dimensional linear Green equation.

MEASURES AND ORIGINAL NORMALIZATION. Let f>0 be real H^s(Y). Define
ν=π_*(fΩ), c=M/∫YfΩ,
and assume ||cf−fε||_{H^s}≤δ. The normalized density difference g=cf−fε has zero Ω-integral, so the contraction applies. Set U=v0+w and u=U∘π^{-1}−sup_YU. Explicit disk lifting proves the genuine equation
MA_ext,h(u)=cν, sup_Xu=0.
All wedges retain dd^c=(i/(2π))∂bar∂ and have no divided volume factorial. Near the cusp α=0 and η=ρκ1, so
π*h^n=n! ρ κ1∧…∧κn,
Ω=n! λ κ1∧…∧κn.
Thus on Xreg near its singular divisor,
ν=(fλ/ρ)h^n,
with ρ=(4|z|^2+9|z|^4)/a if κ1=(i/(2π))a dz∧dbar z. The reciprocal cusp/Jacobian factor remains precisely λ/ρ. Generic degree is one; no finite-degree factor is missing. The singular divisor has zero ν-mass. Non-pluripolarity and finiteness follow as in n6. Densities fε+t∏_{j=1}^n cos(2πxj), with nonzero small t, give explicit full-variable compact examples.

MASS IN THE ENTIRE BOUNDED TYPE. If W is any bounded canonical H-psh function, expand
(H+dd^cW)^n=Σ_{r=0}^n binom(n,r)H^{n−r}∧(dd^cW)^r.
The bounded-product recursion and compact Stokes give, for r≥1,
∫H^{n−r}∧(dd^cW)^r=∫W dd^c(H^{n−r})∧(dd^cW)^{r−1}=0.
Consequently every bounded potential has finite mass
∫(H+dd^cW)^n=∫H^n=M=∫k^n.
The type downstairs is ordinary type zero: all bounded genuine canonical h-psh functions, not just small or smooth potentials.

ALL-BOUNDED UNIQUENESS. Let U be any bounded canonical k-psh solution with the same measure as the constructed C^2 solution V, and put A=k+dd^cU, B=k+dd^cV≥βK0. Apply torus convolution to U,V,k, exactly as in n3. The convolved k_j retains its surface-pullback torsion, hence dd^ck_j=0 and dk_j∧d^ck_j=0. Set
A_j=k_j+dd^cU_j, B_j=k_j+dd^cV_j,
φ_j=U_j−V_j,
T_j=Σ_{r=0}^{n−1} A_j^r∧B_j^{n−1−r}.
Then A_j,B_j≥0, B_j≥βK0, and
A_j^n−B_j^n=dd^cφ_j∧T_j.
Every A_j and B_j has the same d- and d^c-derivatives as k_j. The Leibniz formula for dd^c of each monomial in T_j contains only dd^ck_j or dk_j∧d^ck_j as derivative factors, so dd^cT_j=0. The scalar-square identity yields
−∫φ_j(A_j^n−B_j^n)=∫dφ_j∧d^cφ_j∧T_j
≥β^{n−1}∫dφ_j∧d^cφ_j∧K0^{n−1}.
The weighted convergence reconstructed in n5, applied to local closed positive shifts and expansions, makes the left side tend to zero. Fourier Poincaré shows U−V is constant. Mass first forces equality of equation constants. Subtracting v0 transfers the assertion to the H-background, and the normalization homeomorphism transfers it to the entire bounded downstairs class. This is the full-class uniqueness argument in every dimension n≥2, not merely elliptic uniqueness in the contraction ball.

DESCENT, REGULARITY AND REFINEMENTS. U∈H^{s+2} is C^1 (indeed C^2) upstairs. The explicit cusp inverse estimate of n2 gives local Hölder exponent 1/3 for the full potential u in local embedding coordinates downstairs, unchanged upon adding the other smooth factors. There are no poles and no residual is substituted for the potential. On Xreg u is at least C^2. Every further resolution factors through this explicit normalization; the constructed pullback is constant on all compact fibers with finite canonical values. Extended products are unchanged under common refinements by the supplied product background and biholomorphic locality. Degenerate pulled-back metrics remain explicitly acknowledged as degenerate.

LIMITATION. This result depends on ordinary foundational bounded BT decreasing continuity, with the stronger weighted variant now independently proved in n5. Its literal primary-source audit remains the outstanding completion item described in n6. The package is not a classification, does not treat pole types, and does not cover arbitrary data. Apart from that sharply isolated foundational audit, all new geometry, n-dimensional solvability, normalization, entire-type mass and uniqueness, descent and Hölder continuity have explicit proofs.

This validates both all-bounded mass conservation and the torsion-free energy identity in arbitrary dimension.
