If ||cf−f_ε||_{H^s}≤δ_0, the resulting w with g=cf−f_ε gives U=v_0+w and u=U∘π^{−1}−sup_YU satisfying MA_ext,h(u)=cν and sup_Xu=0. The datum is finite positive and non-pluripolar and has zero mass on the singular divisor. The data may vary in all 2n real variables, and the full degree-n Monge–Ampère polynomial is involved.
Assuming the declared foundational bounded Bedford–Taylor calculus and decreasing continuity, every bounded canonical H-plurisubharmonic W has ∫_Y(H+δW)^n=∫_YH^n=∫_Yk^n=M. Ordinary type zero downstairs is the entire class of bounded genuine canonical h-plurisubharmonic functions. Every member has finite total extended mass M. Any two solutions for the displayed datum in this entire class have the same equation constant and differ by a constant at every canonical value; normalized solutions are therefore unique. In particular the uniqueness is not restricted to regular potentials or to the radius-R ball.
The full potential u is finite everywhere, locally Hölder 1/3 in local embedding coordinates on X, and at least C^2 on X_reg. There are no poles and no residual is substituted for u. Every resolution of X factors through Y, and the constructed pullback is literally constant on every compact fiber with its finite canonical value. Equations, measures, and the bounded type are independent of resolutions and common refinements. Pulled-back backgrounds on refinements may be degenerate.
All wedges use δ with no divided-volume factorial. On X_reg near the cusp, where α=0, H^n=n!ρ κ_1∧⋯∧κ_n and Ω=n!λ κ_1∧⋯∧κ_n, hence ν=[(fλ/ρ)∘π^{−1}]h^n. If κ_1=(i/(2π))a dz∧dbar z, then ρ=(4|z|^2+9|z|^4)/a there. The map has degree one, so there is no additional finite-degree factor, and the singular divisor contributes no mass. Smooth densities f=f_ε+t∏_{j=1}^n cos(2πx_j), for sufficiently small nonzero t in periodic real coordinates, give nontrivial compact examples with c=1. This package concerns only the stated cuspidal-product geometry, surface-supported torsion, bounded ordinary type, and perturbative data; it does not treat arbitrary unibranch spaces, arbitrary data, or types with poles.
reconstruction.proof:
The curve, its normalization and the disk-lifting argument are those of w7-1/n1. Taking products with the remaining elliptic curves preserves compactness, connectedness, reducedness, local irreducibility and pure dimension. The normalization remains finite, bijective, degree one and a homeomorphism. Its singular locus and the upstairs divisor are as stated; every disk lifts by lifting its first coordinate and leaving the others unchanged.

The forms involving the first factor, and α involving the first two factors, have exactly the properties proved in w7-1/n1. The extra flat summands are closed. The support of α is separated from D, so the two operator norms are finite. The prescribed smallness gives h positive in the local-embedding sense, H≥H_0/2 off D, H=H_0 of rank n−1 on D, and k≥K_0/2. It gives dh≠0 because dα≠0 on the regular locus. The Fourier solution v of the first-factor equation gives k=K_0+εα exactly.

Here are the stronger differential identities essential in dimension n>2. The only nonclosed part is α, pulled back from a complex surface. Thus δH=δk=0. The three-forms dH,d^cH,dk,d^ck are pulled back from that surface, and their indicated wedge products have real degree six there, so vanish. For an even-degree form K,
δ(K^r)=r δK∧K^{r−1}+r(r−1)dK∧d^cK∧K^{r−2}.
Consequently δ(H^r)=δ(k^r)=0. The same identities hold after torus convolution: the nonclosed part still comes from the first two factors and its δ remains zero. They also imply δ(A^aB^b)=0 for smooth A=k_j+δP and B=k_j+δQ: all their first derivatives are those of k_j, and every cross torsion term vanishes on the surface. This is more restrictive than pluriclosedness alone.

Use Fourier Sobolev spaces on the real 2n-torus. The nonconstant symbol of L_0 is a negative definite quadratic form, so L_0:H^{s+2}_0→H^s_0 is invertible with finite bound A_0. Expanding k^{n−1} gives a polynomial in ε with smooth coefficients. Differentiation followed by multiplication by these coefficients is bounded H^{s+2}→H^s. Summing its coefficient bounds on |ε|≤ε_0 gives B_{n,s} and the stated estimate. Integration by parts against δ(k^{n−1})=0 proves that L_ε has zero integral. The geometric-series inverse of I+L_0^−1(L_ε−L_0) has norm at most two under the stated smallness; hence the inverse bound A=2A_0 is valid.

The elementary Fourier algebra estimate holds for s>n: ||ab||_{H^s}≤C||a||_{H^s}||b||_{H^s}. It follows by weighted convolution and the summability of (1+|m|²)^−s on Z^{2n}. Smooth multiplication has the corresponding boundedness. Applying these estimates to the finite polynomial Q_ε gives its quadratic and Lipschitz bounds on the unit ball, uniformly on the compact ε interval. Fourier summability for second derivatives gives D_{n,s}. For smooth w and r≥1,
∫k^{n−r}∧(δw)^r=∫δ(W_r^*)∧k^{n−r}=0,
where W_r^*=w(δw)^{r−1}; its Hessian is (δw)^r and δ(k^{n−r})=0. Sobolev density extends this zero-integral identity to the specified w. Thus the inverse and nonlinear map act on zero-mean spaces.

On the radius-R ball set T(w)=L_ε^−1(g−Q_ε(w)). Its norm is at most R/2+AC_{n,s}R²≤3R/4 and its Lipschitz constant is at most 2AC_{n,s}R≤1/2. Iteration gives a fixed point. Expanding (k+δw)^n gives the desired equation, and D_{n,s}R≤1/4 gives k+δw≥K_0/4. The hypothesis s≥n+3 ensures H^{s+2}⊂C², by summing its differentiated Fourier series.

Before treating the normalized datum, we prove the mass and rough uniqueness claims using only the bounded calculus in the supports. For a bounded canonical K-plurisubharmonic W, with K=H or k, use simultaneous torus convolution W_j,K_j. As in the proof of w7-1/n3, local quadratic shifts W_j+q+b r_j² decrease to W+q. The ordinary and weighted convergence in w7-1/n5, and the bounded calculus in w7-1/n3, therefore give convergence of all expanded powers and their bounded-potential weighted versions. For smooth W_j, expansion and Stokes give
∫(K_j+δW_j)^n=∫K_j^n,
since every other term integrates to zero against δ(K_j^{n−r})=0. Passing to the limit proves ∫(K+δW)^n=∫K^n. Bounded local truncations are stationary, so this is the extended mass. Applying the smooth calculation to v_0 gives ∫H^n=∫k^n=M>0.

For uniqueness let P be any bounded canonical k-plurisubharmonic competitor and V the constructed C² solution, with B=k+δV≥βK_0. Suppose A^n=B^n, where A=k+δP. Convolve simultaneously and put t_j=P_j−V_j and
T_j=Σ_{a=0}^{n−1} A_j^a∧B_j^{n−1−a}.
Here A_j≥0, B_j≥βK_0, δT_j=0 by the torsion calculation above, and T_j≥B_j^{n−1}. Therefore
∫t_j(A_j^n−B_j^n)=−∫dt_j∧d^ct_j∧T_j
≤−β^{n−1}∫dt_j∧d^ct_j∧K_0^{n−1}.
The equality follows from δ(t_j²) and Stokes. Weighted convergence applies after expanding each mixed power into local Hessian products and smooth coefficients, shifting each weight by its fixed quadratic; it makes the left side tend to ∫(P−V)(A^n−B^n)=0. Hence the uniformly elliptic gradient energy tends to zero. Fourier Poincaré and convergence of convolution in L² make P−V constant almost everywhere. Local canonical quasi-plurisubharmonic representatives are determined by their almost-everywhere values, so the difference is constant everywhere. This argument places no Sobolev or smallness condition on P.

For f in the statement, c∫fΩ=M gives g=cf−f_ε zero mean. The data hypothesis permits the construction. U=v_0+w has H+δU=k+δw. Disk lifting proves genuine descent, and the homeomorphism gives finite continuous values. The pushforward equation is exactly MA_ext,h(u)=cπ*(fΩ). The volume fΩ is finite and zero on D; local genuine plurisubharmonic pole sets pull back to ordinary plurisubharmonic pole sets of zero volume. Thus ν is non-pluripolar with zero singular-divisor mass. Ordinary type zero downstairs is precisely all bounded genuine canonical h-plurisubharmonic functions. Every one pulls back to a bounded H-plurisubharmonic function and has mass M, forcing its equation constant to be c. Pushforward by the Borel homeomorphism is injective on measures. Subtracting v_0 and applying the rough uniqueness just proved yields uniqueness against the entire bounded class.

The inverse cusp estimate proved in w7-1/n2 uses only |z²−z′²| and |z³−z′³|, so it applies with all extra product coordinates unchanged. The C² function U is locally Lipschitz upstairs; thus its full descent is locally Hölder 1/3 and C² on X_reg. All its values are finite and canonical. There are no poles or substituted residuals.

Every smooth resolution factors through Y by the normalization argument in w7-1/n3, which is unchanged by extra factors. Under a further modification, local bounded products agree off analytic exceptional sets, and none charges those sets by the bounded non-pluripolar calculus. Consequently their pushforwards agree. Composition pullbacks are literally constant on resolution fibers since π is injective. This proves descent and refinement independence without asserting positivity of a pulled-back metric.

Finally π has degree one. On the regular locus near the cusp α=0, so H^n=n!ρ κ_1∧...∧κ_n and Ω=n!λ κ_1∧...∧κ_n. Change of variables on its biholomorphic regular part gives the displayed density fλ/ρ relative to h^n. If κ_1=(i/(2π))a dz∧dbar z, the cusp calculation gives ρ=(4|z|²+9|z|⁴)/a. Neither divisor carries datum mass. The product G=∏cos(2πx_j) is smooth, nonzero and zero mean. Small nonzero t gives positive f=f_ε+tG, c=1 and a nonconstant correction, since a constant correction would leave f_ε unchanged. All hypotheses and conclusions are confined to this geometry, surface-supported torsion, bounded type and perturbative data.

notes.summary: Complete scoped candidate in every complex dimension n≥2: cuspidally pinch one elliptic factor of a flat torus, use an explicitly small genuinely nonclosed surface-supported perturbation of an ambient Hermitian background, and prescribe any positive H^s normalization density sufficiently close after mass normalization to an explicit reference. Proves nonlinear existence, fixed finite mass and constant-difference uniqueness in the entire bounded canonical type, full-potential Hölder continuity downstairs, actual disk/fiber descent, exact degree-one/Jacobian normalization, and common-refinement stability.
notes.detailedSummary: For X=C×E^{n−1}, where C is a one-point cuspidal pinching of a square elliptic curve and π:E^n→X is its degree-one normalization homeomorphism, construct h=hC+Σκj+ε(∂A∧bar∂B+bar∂A∧∂B), A supported away from the cusp, B on the second factor, with dα≠0. Explicit relative-norm and Fourier-operator bounds allow nonzero ε and ensure ambient positivity of h without pretending π*h is positive: H=π*h has rank n−1 on the cusp divisor. A one-factor Fourier primitive v0 repairs H to k=K0+εα≥K0/2. Because torsion is pulled from two complex factors, dd^c k=0 and dk∧d^c k=0, hence all powers and the mixed energy forms are dd^c-closed. For integer s≥n+3, Neumann inversion of the full n-dimensional linearization and a Sobolev polynomial contraction solve every positive normalized density cf within an explicitly defined H^s radius of fε=k^n/K0^n, with c=M/∫fK0^n and M=∫H^n=∫k^n. The class is ordinary type zero: all bounded genuine canonical h-psh potentials, not only the contraction ball. Bounded recursion gives finite mass M for the entire class. Simultaneous torus convolution and the audited/reconstructed weighted BT limit give an energy identity proving uniqueness against every rough member of the class. Explicit lifting of cusp disks and the normalization homeomorphism prove genuine descent; the full solution is locally ambient-Hölder 1/3, finite everywhere, and C² on the regular locus. All resolutions factor through the normalization, and pullbacks are literally constant on compact fibers; exceptional sets carry no extended mass. Near the cusp ν=(fλ/ρ)h^n, with ρ=4|z|²+9|z|⁴ in the chosen flat normalization, and the singular divisor has zero data mass. The compact example contains no rational curves and is therefore not a projective cone. The theorem is restricted to this geometry, these backgrounds, this bounded type, and this perturbative family of data; it does not classify arbitrary singularities or pole types. The only substantive external input is foundational bounded BT calculus as audited in n1, plus the resolution-product background expressly supplied in the task.
notes.text:
A SUFFICIENT-CONDITION THEOREM WITH NONCLOSED BACKGROUND IN EVERY DIMENSION n≥2.

All occurrences of δ mean dd^c=(i/(2π))∂bar∂. Set d^c=(i/(4π))(bar∂−∂), so δ=d d^c. Products such as h^n have no divided-volume factorial.

THEOREM (precise scope).

Let n≥2 and E=C/(Z+iZ), with κ=(i/(2π))dz∧dbar z. Replace a coordinate disk at a point p of one copy E1 of E by the cusp {y²=x³}, using x=z²,y=z³ on the punctured disk. Denote the resulting compact curve by C, its cusp by q, and its normalization by π1:E1→C. Set
X=C×E2×...×En,  Y=E1×...×En,  π=π1×id.

Choose the background and finite constants by the explicit construction below. In particular h is a positive smooth local-embedding Hermitian background on X with dh≠0; its pullback H is allowed, and shown, to be degenerate. The construction gives a smooth v0 on Y, a positive form k=H+δv0, a fixed flat positive form K0, Ω=K0^n, M=∫Yk^n=∫YH^n>0, and fε=k^n/Ω.

Fix an integer s≥n+3. Choose nonzero ε obeying the relative-positivity and Fourier-operator bounds below, and choose the positive radius δ0 below. For any strictly positive real f∈H^s(Y), let
ν=π_*(fΩ),  c=M/∫YfΩ,
and assume
||cf−fε||_{H^s}≤δ0.

Then there is a genuine canonical h-psh potential u in ordinary type zero satisfying
MA_ext,h(u)=cν,  sup_Xu=0.
The measure ν is finite positive and non-pluripolar. Every potential in the entire ordinary type-zero class has finite total extended mass M. Any two solutions in that entire class have constant difference; hence the displayed normalized solution is unique. This uniqueness is not restricted to smooth potentials or to the perturbative ball.

The actual potential u, not a residual, is finite everywhere and continuous, locally Hölder 1/3 in local embedding coordinates on X, and at least C² on X_reg. There are no poles in this specified type. Descent and compact-fiber constancy are explicitly proved below. Equations and the bounded singularity type are stable under every resolution and common refinement.

These are sufficient conditions for this particular cuspidal-product geometry, surface-supported nonclosed backgrounds, and perturbative family of data. They make no claim about arbitrary unibranch singularities, arbitrary measures, or prescribed types with poles.

PROOF AND CONSTRUCTION.

1. The compact singular space and its maps.

The cusp parameterization z↦(z²,z³) is finite, injective, and a homeomorphism onto the cusp chart. Locally z is integral because z²=x, and the cusp local ring is C{z²,z³}, a domain with one analytic branch. Gluing the cusp chart to E1 minus p on the punctured coordinate disk gives a compact reduced locally irreducible curve C. The underlying topology is that of E1. The proper bijective map π1 is its normalization and is a biholomorphism away from p.

Thus X is compact, connected, reduced, locally irreducible, and pure of complex dimension n. Its singular locus is {q}×E^{n−1}. The smooth torus Y is a resolution, and π is finite birational of generic degree ONE and a homeomorphism. Write D={p}×E^{n−1}.

Every holomorphic disk into X lifts holomorphically to Y. In a cusp chart a disk has x,y with y²=x³. If x is not identically zero, z=y/x off its zeros satisfies z²=x,z³=y and |z|²=|x|. It is bounded at each omitted point and extends holomorphically by the one-variable removable-singularity argument. If x is identically zero, so is y, and the first lifted component is constantly p. The other components are unchanged. Uniqueness follows from injectivity of π, so the local lifts glue.

2. Ambient positivity, genuine nonclosedness, and explicit repair of degeneracy.

Choose an ambient-smooth positive metric hC on C that equals
δ(|x|²+|y|²)
near q. One concrete construction uses this form in the cusp chart and the flat metric transferred from E1 on C_reg, with a smooth local-embedding cutoff equal to one on a smaller cusp chart and zero outside a larger one. The convex combination is positive on the smooth curve; near q it has the given strictly positive ambient extension. On overlaps away from q a positive tangent metric has a positive ambient extension, for example by adding a positive normal metric in a local embedding. This gives the required local-embedding background.

Its pullback η=π1*hC is smooth, nonnegative, positive off p, and near p
η=(4|z|²+9|z|⁴)κ1.
Write η=ρκ1 on E1 and put
λ=(∫E1η)/(∫E1κ1)>0.
Here ρ is smooth, nonnegative, and vanishes precisely at p. On Y put
H0=η+Σ_{j=2}^nκj,  K0=λκ1+Σ_{j=2}^nκj.
H0 is closed but has rank n−1 on D. This pullback is NOT a positive Hermitian metric on Y.

Choose a real smooth A on C supported away from q, and a real smooth B on E2. On X let
α=∂A∧bar∂B+bar∂A∧∂B,
with all omitted factors pulled back. It is a real ambient-smooth (1,1)-form and vanishes near the singular locus. It obeys
α=∂(A bar∂B)+bar∂(A∂B),
so δα=0. But it need not be closed:
∂α=−∂A∧∂bar∂B+∂bar∂A∧∂B.
For explicit choices take A to be a local real quadratic times a cutoff at some r∈C_reg, so ∂A(r)=0 and ∂bar∂A(r)≠0; take B to be a real linear coordinate times a cutoff at s∈E2, so ∂B(s)≠0. Then ∂α(r,s)≠0, hence dα≠0.

Let α also denote its pullback to Y when no confusion is possible, and define
rH=sup_{Y\D}||α||_{H0,op},  rK=sup_Y||α||_{K0,op}.
Both are finite: α vanishes near D. Select a fixed ε0>0 so that ε0≤1 and ε0rH,ε0rK<1/2. Later impose an additional explicit smallness bound on nonzero ε with |ε|≤ε0. Then
h=hC+Σ_{j=2}^nκj+εα
is a positive smooth local-embedding Hermitian background. Near the cusp α=0; elsewhere positivity follows from the relative norm bound. It is genuinely nonclosed, since dh=εdα≠0 on X_reg. Upstairs
H=π*h=H0+εα
is still rank n−1 on D and smooth nonnegative everywhere.

Solve the mean-zero first-factor equation
δv=(λ−ρ)κ1
on E1 by Fourier division. In the square elliptic coordinate the operator δ/κ1 is (1/4) times the Euclidean Laplacian, with nonzero-mode eigenvalues −π²|m|². The right side has zero integral. Divide every nonzero coefficient by this eigenvalue and set the zero coefficient to zero. Rapid coefficient decay proves v is smooth real. Define v0=pr1*v. Then
k=H+δv0=K0+εα≥K0/2.
Thus genuine positivity upstairs has been proved by an explicit potential; it has not been incorrectly attributed to π*h.

3. The special torsion identity, in all dimensions.

The derivatives of H and k come only from α, pulled back from E1×E2. Therefore
δH=δk=0,  dH∧d^cH=dk∧d^ck=0.
The second identity holds because the two factors are 3-forms from a real four-dimensional source. The Leibniz rule consequently gives
δ(H^r)=δ(k^r)=0 for every r≥0.
Equivalently, in ∂,bar∂ notation every derivative term has either ∂bar∂k or ∂k∧bar∂k as a factor, and both vanish. The same assertion holds for H. This is stronger than merely pluriclosedness when n≥3, and is a decisive restriction of the theorem. A generic nonclosed pluriclosed metric in higher dimension is not being covered.

4. Full n-dimensional nonlinear solvability, reconstructed by Fourier estimates.

Use Fourier Sobolev norms on the real 2n-dimensional square torus. Zero mean refers to Ω=K0^n, a constant positive volume multiple. Let H^s_0 be the real zero-mean space. Define
Lεw=n k^{n−1}∧δw/Ω,
L0w=n K0^{n−1}∧δw/Ω.
Because δ(k^{n−1})=0, compact integration by parts gives ∫LεwΩ=0.

Write b1=λ,b2=...=bn=1. Then
L0=Σ_{j=1}^n b_j^{-1}∂²/(∂z_j∂bar z_j).
Its symbol on a nonzero mode m∈Z^{2n} is
ℓ(m)=−π²Σ_j b_j^{-1}(m_{2j−1}²+m_{2j}²).
Fourier division proves L0:H^{s+2}_0→H^s_0 has a bounded inverse. One may take
A0=sup_{m≠0}(1+|m|²)/|ℓ(m)|<∞.
In particular A0≤2 max_j b_j/π².

All remaining linearization constants are defined before solving the equation. Expand
Lε−L0=Σ_{j=1}^{n−1} ε^j P_j,
P_jw=n binom(n−1,j) K0^{n−1−j}∧α^j∧δw/Ω.
Let E_j be an upper bound for ||P_j||_{H^{s+2}→H^s}, and set
B_{n,s}=Σ_{j=1}^{n−1} ε0^{j−1}E_j.
These are finite coefficient bounds: α is fixed smooth, differentiation maps H^{s+2} to H^s, and smooth multiplication is bounded by its Fourier coefficient norms. Impose
|ε|A0B_{n,s}≤1/2.
A nonzero such ε always exists. The Neumann series for I+L0^{-1}(Lε−L0) converges in operator norm and proves that Lε is invertible on the zero-mean spaces, with inverse bound A=2A0. This is a proved linear solvability statement, not a geometric assumption that an unknown nonlinear solution exists.

Expand the full degree-n determinant polynomial as
(k+δw)^n/Ω=fε+Lεw+Qε(w),
Qε(w)=Σ_{r=2}^n binom(n,r) k^{n−r}∧(δw)^r/Ω.
For s>n the Fourier Sobolev space H^s is an algebra. Indeed Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the ℓ¹ norm of Fourier coefficients by the H^s norm because Σ_m(1+|m|²)^{-s}<∞, and the weighted convolution inequality gives the product estimate. Repeated application to this finite polynomial gives a finite known constant C_{n,s}, uniform for |ε|≤ε0, such that on the unit H^{s+2} ball
||Qε(w)||_{H^s}≤C_{n,s}||w||_{H^{s+2}}²,
||Qε(w)−Qε(z)||_{H^s}≤C_{n,s}(||w||+||z||)||w−z||.
The norms on the right are H^{s+2}. The constant can be obtained directly by summing the finite wedge combinatorics, the H^s algebra constant, and the fixed coefficient norms of k^{n−r}/Ω.

There is no hidden mean obstruction. For smooth w and r≥1,
∫Y k^{n−r}∧(δw)^r
=∫Y w δ(k^{n−r})∧(δw)^{r−1}=0.
The other factor is closed, so there are no cross-derivative terms in this integration by parts. Fourier-polynomial approximation extends it to H^{s+2}. In particular Qε maps to H^s_0.

Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz also gives a finite bound D_{n,s} such that
||δw||_{L∞,K0}≤D_{n,s}||w||_{H^{s+2}}.
The relevant coefficient sum converges since s>n. Choose
0<R≤min(1,(4AC_{n,s})^{-1},(4D_{n,s})^{-1}),
δ0=R/(2A).
For g∈H^s_0 with ||g||≤δ0, the map
T(w)=Lε^{-1}(g−Qε(w))
takes the closed radius-R ball into itself: its image norm is at most R/2+R/4. Its Lipschitz constant there is at most 2AC_{n,s}R≤1/2. Starting with w_0=0, the iterates have geometrically decreasing successive differences, hence converge in the complete Fourier Sobolev space to a fixed point w. It satisfies
(k+δw)^n=(fε+g)Ω,
k+δw≥K0/2−K0/4=K0/4.
The Fourier estimates also yield H^{s+2}⊂C² and H^s⊂C⁰. The equation is therefore a pointwise equality of continuous positive densities.

For the datum in the theorem, take g=cf−fε. Its mean is zero because c∫fΩ=M=∫fεΩ. It satisfies the stated radius condition, so the preceding construction applies. This is the genuinely n-dimensional nonlinear Monge–Ampère equation: the entire degree-n polynomial Qε is retained, and the data can vary freely in all 2n real variables. The one-dimensional Fourier step of Section 2 only repairs the reference metric and is not the prescribed-data existence argument.

5. Actual downstairs descent, genuine disk values, and continuity.

Set U=v0+w on Y and define
u0=U∘π^{-1},  u=u0−sup_YU.
This notation u0 denotes the potential, not the measure ν. Since π is a homeomorphism and U is C², u is a finite continuous function on X. For any disk f into X, let f~ be its explicit holomorphic lift. With the local p_f required in the question,
δ(U∘f~+p_f)=f~*(H+δU)=f~*(k+δw)≥0.
Thus u obeys the actual disk definition of h-psh. Its finite values are the canonical upper values; none has been set by an arbitrary null-set modification. Constant subtraction does not affect the equation, and sup_Xu=0.

The cusp inverse has local ambient Hölder exponent 1/3. To verify it for arbitrary pairs z,z', put d=z−z', a=z+z'. Then
z²−z'²=da,
z³−z'³=d(3a²+d²)/4.
If |a|≥|d|/4, the first difference controls |d|² and hence |d|³ on a bounded small chart. If |a|<|d|/4, the second has magnitude at least 13|d|³/64. Hence
|z−z'|≤C(|z²−z'²|+|z³−z'³|)^{1/3}.
Together with the other smooth coordinates and the local Lipschitz bound for U, this proves the asserted local Hölder continuity of the FULL potential u in local embedding coordinates. Its regularity on X_reg is inherited from the biholomorphic normalization there and is at least C². No residual is substituted and there are no pole values to reinterpret.

6. The entire specified class and its finite fixed mass.

The reference is ψ=0. Ordinary type zero, with the two inequalities in the question, is exactly the class of all bounded genuine canonical h-psh functions on X. It contains no poles; it is not restricted by a small Sobolev norm.

For any such function a, its pullback W=a∘π is bounded genuine H-psh on Y. To see smooth-domain positivity explicitly, on a coordinate ball add a quadratic q with δq≥H. On every upstairs disk, W+q is subharmonic by the downstairs disk test plus the nonnegative difference δq−H. Thus W+q is a bounded genuine psh function on the smooth ball, and H+δW≥0 as a current. The same reasoning applies to local shifts of every bounded potential used below.

Use the bounded calculus in n1. For r≥1, (δW)^r=δ(W(δW)^{r−1}), and the power (δW)^{r−1} is closed. Compact distributional Stokes gives
∫Y H^{n−r}∧(δW)^r
=∫Y W(δW)^{r−1}∧δ(H^{n−r})=0.
Expand (H+δW)^n to obtain
∫Y(H+δW)^n=∫YH^n.
This proves finite mass for EVERY member of the bounded type, not only the constructed one. Applying the smooth version to v0 shows ∫H^n=∫k^n=M. Positivity and k≥K0/2 show M>0. Because the extended product agrees with the bounded product here, this is exactly the mass of the equation required in the question.

In particular every equation MA_ext,h(a)=c'ν in this type forces c'=M/ν(X)=c. Existence upstairs gives
MA_ext,h(u)=π_*((H+δU)^n)=π_*(cfΩ)=cν.

7. Constant-difference uniqueness against every bounded rough competitor.

It remains to establish uniqueness beyond the contraction ball. Subtract v0 upstairs. The constructed potential becomes V=w, with
B=k+δV≥βK0,  β=1/4.
Let W be the pullback of any other bounded downstairs solution and put Z=W−v0. Then Z is bounded canonical k-psh. Since π is a homeomorphism, its pushforward on finite Borel measures is injective: evaluate a measure on Borel sets π^{-1}(E), or use the Borel inverse map. Thus equality of the downstairs equations, after the preceding mass normalization, implies
A^n=B^n,  A=k+δZ.

Convolve simultaneously on the flat torus with the radial kernels of n1:
Z_j=Z*ρ_j, V_j=V*ρ_j, k_j=k*ρ_j,
A_j=k_j+δZ_j, B_j=k_j+δV_j.
These are smooth positive forms, A_j≥0, B_j≥βK0. Positivity follows by convolution of the positive matrix-valued currents. We have k_j→k smoothly and V_j→V in C². Its torsion still comes only from E1×E2; averaging translations does not add dependence on the other factors.

Let φ_j=Z_j−V_j and
T_j=Σ_{r=0}^{n−1} A_j^r∧B_j^{n−1−r}.
Then A_j^n−B_j^n=δφ_j∧T_j. Moreover δT_j=0. Indeed dA_j=dB_j=dk_j and d^cA_j=d^cB_j=d^ck_j. In the Leibniz differentiation of any mixed monomial, all terms contain either δk_j or dk_j∧d^ck_j, both zero. This is exactly why the surface-supported torsion restriction works in higher dimension.

For a real smooth φ,
δ(φ²)=2φδφ+2dφ∧d^cφ.
Integrate against T_j, use compact Stokes and δT_j=0, and obtain
−∫Y φ_j(A_j^n−B_j^n)
=∫Y dφ_j∧d^cφ_j∧T_j
≥β^{n−1}∫Y dφ_j∧d^cφ_j∧K0^{n−1}.
No d-closedness of T_j was asserted, and no torsion term was dropped: δ-closedness suffices for this scalar-square identity.

Here is the complete limit justification. Choose a fixed local quadratic q dominating k and its convolutions. As in n1, Z_j+q+br_j² is a locally uniformly bounded decreasing psh sequence converging to the canonical Z+q. Expand A_j^n relative to its closed positive Hessian and the smoothly converging form k_j−δq. The unweighted and reconstructed weighted BT limits of n1 give
∫Z_jA_j^n→∫ZA^n,
∫V_jA_j^n→∫VA^n.
The second also follows from unweighted convergence and uniform convergence of V_j. Since B_j^n→B^n uniformly as densities, bounded dominated convergence gives
∫Z_jB_j^n→∫ZB^n,
∫V_jB_j^n→∫VB^n.
Local partitions of unity patch these statements. Vanishing constants br_j² do not change the Hessians and disappear in weighted integrals. Consequently the left side of the energy identity tends to
−∫(Z−V)(A^n−B^n)=0.
The positive flat Dirichlet energy of φ_j tends to zero.

Fourier Poincaré now shows that φ_j converges in L² to a constant, since the energy controls all nonzero Fourier modes. Bounded canonical regularization also gives φ_j→Z−V in L², and convolution preserves the mean. Thus Z−V is constant almost everywhere. Adding the same local quadratic makes both functions psh; equal-a.e. psh functions have identical canonical representatives, since their canonical local averages agree. Therefore Z−V is that constant at EVERY point, including D. Returning to H and then using π proves the constant-difference statement downstairs with genuine canonical values. Supremum normalization makes that constant zero.

This argument compares every bounded rough solution with the regular solution constructed above. It therefore proves uniqueness in the entire specified ordinary class, not merely among smooth solutions or nearby solutions.

8. Data, degree/Jacobian factors, and exceptional behavior.

The data transformation is exactly ν=π_*(fΩ), with generic degree one. There is no division by an unstated finite degree. Its total mass is ∫YfΩ, so the original equation constant is c=M/ν(X).

On X_reg, let J=H^n/Ω>0, regarded as a function upstairs. The full change-of-measure formula is
ν|_{X_reg}=[(f/J)∘π^{-1}] h^n.
It is simply change of variables under the biholomorphic part of this degree-one normalization. Near the cusp α=0, and in the specified flat coordinate
ρ=4|z|²+9|z|⁴,
H^n=n!ρ κ1∧...∧κn,
Ω=n!λ κ1∧...∧κn.
Thus there the density is precisely (fλ/ρ)∘π^{-1} relative to h^n. This reciprocal degeneracy/Jacobian factor is not omitted, and the original δ normalization is retained. The singular divisor has zero ν mass because its inverse image D has Ω-measure zero. We interpret h^n downstairs as its regular-locus volume extended with zero mass on that divisor.

The measure is finite because f is continuous on compact Y. To verify its non-pluripolarity directly, pull a local nontrivial genuine psh function defining a pluripolar set back through π. Disk tests make the pullback psh on Y; it is not identically −∞ on the corresponding connected neighborhood, since π is an onto homeomorphism. Its pole set is Lebesgue null by local integrability of nontrivial psh functions. The measure fΩ gives it zero mass. This proves ν is non-pluripolar without a prescribed-data Monge–Ampère theorem.

For any further modification μ:Z'→Y the measure transformation is
μ_*MA_{μ*H}(W∘μ)=MA_H(W)
for bounded canonical W as above. Off an analytic exceptional/image set it is the usual biholomorphic change of variables (generic degree one, with the ordinary coordinate Jacobian already contained in the pulled-back top form). The extended products assign zero mass to the exceptional analytic set and to its analytic image. There is therefore no exceptional contribution. No finite map of degree greater than one or hidden ramification correction is used in this construction.

9. All resolutions, actual fiber constancy, and class independence.

Every smooth resolution σ:Z'→X factors through π. This can be checked directly near the cusp: pull back x,y and, where x≠0, set z=y/x. It satisfies z²=x,z³=y and is locally bounded by |z|²=|x|. A bounded holomorphic function on the complement of an analytic hypersurface in a smooth coordinate ball extends holomorphically, by the removable-singularity/Cauchy argument on coordinate slices. This extends z and produces the factor map μ:Z'→Y. The lifts are unique and glue. The map μ is proper birational and σ=π∘μ.

For the constructed solution its pullback is literally U∘μ−sup_YU. It is constant on each compact μ-fiber, with its finite canonical value, because it is a composition. Since the normalization fibers are singletons, this proves the required compact-fiber constancy for σ as well. Nothing is inferred about descent merely from a measure equation upstairs.

The measure identity of Section 8 gives σ_*MA_{σ*h}(u∘σ)=MA_ext,h(u) and the same assertion for bounded competitors. Applying it on a common refinement proves complete independence of the choice of resolution. Forms μ*H and μ*k may be degenerate; they are never labeled positive metrics. Local bounded psh shifts, rather than false strict positivity of a pullback, justify their products.

The ordinary inequalities defining type zero are preserved under every surjective pullback and recovered by surjectivity. All functions have finite canonical values; no subtraction of common −∞ values occurs. Thus the specified singularity type is stable under common refinements as well as the measure equation.

10. A nontrivial compact example, and why it is beyond projective cones.

For any n≥2 take the explicit E, C, quadratic-cutoff A, and linear-cutoff B above. Choose any nonzero ε satisfying the finite stated bounds. Define the mean-zero smooth function on Y
G=∏_{j=1}^n cos(2πx_j)+∏_{j=1}^n cos(2πy_j),
where z_j=x_j+iy_j. For sufficiently small nonzero t,
f=fε+tG
is positive and ||tG||_{H^s}≤δ0. Since ∫GΩ=0, ∫fΩ=M and c=1. The theorem solves the prescribed datum π_*(fΩ); it was not defined from an unknown solution. The resulting correction w cannot be constant because G≠0. More generally the theorem admits every positive full-variable H^s perturbation in the normalized ball, not only this illustrative polynomial.

These spaces are not projective cones. Every map P¹→X lifts locally, hence globally by uniqueness, to Y. The flat holomorphic one-forms dz_j on Y pull back to zero on P¹, so the lifted derivative vanishes and the map is constant. Thus X contains no nonconstant rational curves. A nontrivial projective cone of positive dimension contains its ruling projective lines. This also separates the example geometrically from cone constructions, not merely by renaming the local equation.

The normalization step repairs degeneracy explicitly, the prescribed-data step is genuinely nonlinear in dimension n≥2, and the rough energy step proves entire-bounded-class uniqueness. Continuity is obtained directly downstairs through the cusp inverse, not by invoking a log-terminal theorem (the spaces here are nonnormal). These conclusions finish the stated sufficient-condition problem within the exact scope of the theorem.

reconstruction.statement:
Let δ=dd^c=(i/(2π))∂bar∂ and d^c=(i/(4π))(bar∂−∂). All wedge powers below have no divided-volume factorial. The following sufficient-condition theorem holds for every integer n≥2.

Geometry and background. Let E=C/(Z+iZ), let E_1,…,E_n be copies of E with κ_j=(i/(2π))dz_j∧dbar z_j, and choose p∈E_1. Replace a coordinate disk at p by the cusp y^2=x^3, using x=z^2,y=z^3 on the punctured disk; call the resulting curve C and its cusp q. Its normalization π_1:E_1→C is finite, bijective, of generic degree one, a homeomorphism, and a biholomorphism away from p. Set X=C×E_2×⋯×E_n, Y=E_1×⋯×E_n, π=π_1×id, and D={p}×E_2×⋯×E_n. Then X is connected, compact, reduced, locally irreducible, and pure of complex dimension n, with singular locus {q}×E_2×⋯×E_n. The smooth torus Y is a resolution, and every holomorphic disk into X has a unique holomorphic lift to Y.
Choose a smooth positive local-embedding Hermitian form h_C on C equal to δ(|x|^2+|y|^2) near q. Its pullback η=π_1^*h_C is smooth, nonnegative, positive off p, and equals (4|z|^2+9|z|^4)κ_1 near p. Write η=ρκ_1 and λ=(∫_{E_1}η)/(∫_{E_1}κ_1)>0. Thus ρ is smooth, nonnegative, and vanishes precisely at p. Put H_0=η+Σ_{j=2}^nκ_j and K_0=λκ_1+Σ_{j=2}^nκ_j.
Choose real smooth A on C supported away from q and real smooth B on E_2, with points r∈C_reg and s_0∈E_2 such that ∂A(r)=0, ∂bar∂A(r)≠0, and ∂B(s_0)≠0. Define α=∂A∧bar∂B+bar∂A∧∂B on X, pulled back from C×E_2. It is real and ambient-smooth, vanishes near the singular locus, satisfies δα=0, and has dα≠0. Use α also for its pullback to Y. The constants r_H=sup_{Y\D}||α||_{H_0,op} and r_K=sup_Y||α||_{K_0,op} are finite. Fix ε_0∈(0,1] with ε_0r_H,ε_0r_K<1/2. For nonzero real ε with |ε|≤ε_0, let h=h_C+Σ_{j=2}^nκ_j+εα and H=π^*h. Then h is a smooth strictly positive local-embedding Hermitian background with dh≠0. Its pullback H is smooth nonnegative and has rank n−1 on D; it is not a strictly positive Hermitian metric there.
There is a unique smooth real zero-κ_1-mean v on E_1 with δv=(λ−ρ)κ_1. Let v_0=pr_1^*v. Then k=H+δv_0=K_0+εα≥K_0/2. Both H and k satisfy δH=δk=0 and dH∧d^cH=dk∧d^ck=0, and consequently δ(H^r)=δ(k^r)=0 for every integer r≥0. This is a restriction to torsion supported on the first two complex factors, not merely an assumption of pluriclosedness in arbitrary dimension.

Explicit constants and data hypothesis. Fix an integer s≥n+3, let Ω=K_0^n, M=∫_Yk^n=∫_YH^n>0, and f_ε=k^n/Ω. Use real Fourier Sobolev norms with weights (1+|m|^2)^s, and let H^s_0 be the zero-Ω-mean subspace. Define L_εw=n k^{n−1}∧δw/Ω and L_0w=n K_0^{n−1}∧δw/Ω. Write b_1=λ and b_2=⋯=b_n=1. The operator L_0=Σ_{j=1}^n b_j^{−1}∂^2/(∂z_j∂bar z_j) is invertible from H^{s+2}_0 to H^s_0. On a nonzero Fourier mode m∈Z^{2n}, its symbol is ℓ(m)=−π^2Σ_j b_j^{−1}(m_{2j−1}^2+m_{2j}^2). Take A_0=sup_{m≠0}(1+|m|^2)/|ℓ(m)|, so A_0≤2 max_j b_j/π^2.
For 1≤j≤n−1, define P_jw=n binom(n−1,j)K_0^{n−1−j}∧α^j∧δw/Ω, so L_ε−L_0=Σ_{j=1}^{n−1}ε^jP_j. Choose finite coefficient bounds E_j≥||P_j||_{H^{s+2}→H^s}, and put B_{n,s}=Σ_{j=1}^{n−1}ε_0^{j−1}E_j. Impose the additional geometric smallness condition |ε|A_0B_{n,s}≤1/2. Nonzero ε satisfying all stated bounds exist. Then L_ε:H^{s+2}_0→H^s_0 is invertible with inverse norm at most A=2A_0.
Define Q_ε(w)=Σ_{r=2}^n binom(n,r)k^{n−r}∧(δw)^r/Ω. There are finite constants C_{n,s} and D_{n,s}, determined by the fixed coefficients and Sobolev norms, with C_{n,s} uniform for |ε|≤ε_0, such that on the unit H^{s+2} ball, ||Q_ε(w)||_{H^s}≤C_{n,s}||w||_{H^{s+2}}^2 and ||Q_ε(w)−Q_ε(z)||_{H^s}≤C_{n,s}(||w||_{H^{s+2}}+||z||_{H^{s+2}})||w−z||_{H^{s+2}}, and for every w, ||δw||_{L∞,K_0}≤D_{n,s}||w||_{H^{s+2}}. Each term k^{n−r}∧(δw)^r, r≥1, has zero integral, so L_ε and Q_ε take zero-mean inputs to zero-mean outputs. Choose 0<R≤min{1,(4AC_{n,s})^{−1},(4D_{n,s})^{−1}} and δ_0=R/(2A).
Let f be any strictly positive real H^s function on Y, using its continuous representative. Define ν=π_*(fΩ) and c=M/∫_YfΩ, and assume ||cf−f_ε||_{H^s}≤δ_0. No separability or dependence on only selected factors is required.

Existence, mass, class, and uniqueness. There exists w∈H^{s+2}_0 with ||w||_{H^{s+2}}≤R such that (k+δw)^n=cfΩ and k+δw≥K_0/4. Set U=v_0+w and u=U∘π^{−1}−sup_YU. Then u is a genuine canonical h-plurisubharmonic potential satisfying MA_ext,h(u)=cν and sup_Xu=0. The datum ν is finite, positive, and non-pluripolar.
The specified singularity class is ordinary type of ψ=0: exactly all bounded genuine canonical h-plurisubharmonic functions on X. It is the entire bounded class, not a regularity class or a small Sobolev ball. For every member a, its pullback W=a∘π is bounded canonical H-plurisubharmonic, its bounded product agrees with the task's extended non-pluripolar product, and ∫_Y(H+δW)^n=M. Hence every member has finite total extended mass M. Every equation MA_ext,h(a)=c′ν in this class necessarily has c′=M/ν(X)=c. Any two solutions in the entire class have a constant difference at every point with their canonical values; consequently the supremum-normalized solution is unique, including against all bounded rough competitors.

Actual descent and regularity. The function u is finite everywhere and continuous; its values are canonical, not null-set alterations. For every holomorphic disk f_0 into X, its lift f̃_0 satisfies δ(U∘f̃_0+p_{f_0})=f̃_0^*(H+δU)≥0 whenever δp_{f_0}=f_0^*h. The full potential u, not a residual, is locally Hölder 1/3 in local embedding coordinates and is at least C^2 on X_reg. There are no poles in this class. On a bounded small cusp chart, |z−z′|≤C(|z^2−z′^2|+|z^3−z′^3|)^{1/3} for all z,z′.

Measure transformations and refinements. The map π has generic degree one, ν(X)=∫_YfΩ, and ν assigns zero mass to the singular divisor. Regard h^n as the regular-locus volume extended with zero mass on that divisor. On Y\D put J=H^n/Ω>0. Then ν|_{X_reg}=[(f/J)∘π^{−1}]h^n. Near the cusp, α=0, ρ=4|z|^2+9|z|^4, H^n=n!ρ κ_1∧⋯∧κ_n, and Ω=n!λ κ_1∧⋯∧κ_n, so the density there is exactly (fλ/ρ)∘π^{−1} relative to h^n. There is no missing finite-degree factor and no singular-divisor contribution.
Every smooth resolution σ:Z→X factors as σ=π∘μ through a proper birational modification μ:Z→Y. For every such modification and every bounded canonical H-plurisubharmonic W, μ_*MA_{μ^*H}(W∘μ)=MA_H(W), with no exceptional analytic contribution. Thus σ_*MA_{σ^*h}(u∘σ)=MA_ext,h(u), and the analogous equality holds for every bounded competitor. The constructed pullback is literally U∘μ−sup_YU and is constant with its finite canonical value on every compact σ-fiber. The equation and specified ordinary type are independent of all resolutions and common refinements. Forms μ^*H and μ^*k may be degenerate and are not asserted to be strictly positive. Ordinary bounded-type inequalities are preserved under surjective pullback and recovered by surjectivity.

Nontrivial examples and scope. In the square-torus coordinates z_j=x_j+iy_j, let G=∏_{j=1}^n cos(2πx_j)+∏_{j=1}^n cos(2πy_j). For every sufficiently small nonzero real t, f=f_ε+tG is positive and satisfies ||tG||_{H^s}≤δ_0. It has ∫fΩ=M, so c=1, and its resulting correction w is nonconstant. Every holomorphic map P^1→X is constant; hence these compact spaces contain no nonconstant rational curves and are not nontrivial projective cones. The theorem applies only to the stated cuspidal-product geometry, explicitly small surface-supported nonclosed backgrounds, ordinary bounded type, and perturbative positive H^s data. It does not classify arbitrary unibranch spaces or address arbitrary measures or types with poles. Its external inputs are the declared foundational bounded Bedford–Taylor calculus and the extended-product modification properties stipulated in the task; no desired existence, uniqueness, or downstairs continuity conclusion is an assumption.
reconstruction.proof:
Apply the sufficient-condition construction proved in w7-1/n7 to the square elliptic curves in this statement. We verify the additional explicit constants, hypotheses and transformations, so that none is a hidden solvability or regularity assumption.

The normalization geometry, ambient-positive h_C, smooth coefficient ρ, and disk lifts are those of w7-1/n1 and w7-1/n7. For the present normalization κ_1=(i/(2π))dz_1∧dbar z_1, their cusp calculation is exactly ρ=4|z|²+9|z|⁴. The bump choices of A,B give a real α with δα=0 and dα≠0. Its support is separated from the degenerate divisor, proving finiteness of r_H. Compactness proves finiteness of r_K. The two explicitly imposed inequalities give H≥H_0/2 off D, the unchanged rank n−1 on D, and k≥K_0/2. Near the singular locus the ambient form is unperturbed and strictly positive. Elsewhere positivity is intrinsic on a smooth embedding and has a positive ambient extension. Thus h satisfies precisely the required local-embedding notion, while H is explicitly not positive definite on D. The nonzero ε gives dh≠0.

The mean-zero equation for v is solved by inversion of the first-factor nonconstant Fourier symbols. Smoothness follows from their quadratic growth and the rapid coefficient decay of λ−ρ. This establishes k=K_0+εα rather than presupposing a positive pullback. The torsion calculation in w7-1/n7 shows δH=δk=0 and dH∧d^cH=dk∧d^ck=0, hence all the asserted power identities. In particular the mass identity M=∫k^n=∫H^n follows by smooth expansion and Stokes, and M>0 follows from k>0.

In square-torus coordinates, taking a trace with respect to K_0 gives
L_0w=Σ_j b_j^−1 w_{j bar j},
with no further constant: δw has the same i/(2π) coefficient as κ_j. The mode exp(2πi m·(x,y)) therefore has symbol
ℓ(m)=−π²Σ_j b_j^−1(m_{2j−1}²+m_{2j}²).
It is nonzero exactly when m≠0. The Fourier norm of its inverse from H^s_0 to H^{s+2}_0 is the specified supremum A_0. Since |ℓ(m)|≥π²|m|²/max b_j and (1+|m|²)/|m|²≤2 for nonzero integer m, A_0≤2max b_j/π².

Expansion of (K_0+εα)^{n−1} gives exactly the operators P_j written in the statement. Each is a finite sum of smooth coefficient multiples of second derivatives. Such multiplication is bounded on H^s: Fourier convolution and the summability of weighted Fourier coefficients of a smooth coefficient give a finite multiplier norm. Thus finite E_j bounding the operator norms are available from the fixed coefficients; choosing these bounds invokes no solvability theorem. The displayed definition of B_{n,s} gives
||L_ε−L_0||≤Σ_j|ε|^jE_j≤|ε|B_{n,s}.
Both operators have zero-integral outputs by δ(k^{n−1})=δ(K_0^{n−1})=0. The final geometric smallness condition therefore permits the inverse geometric series on the zero-mean spaces with inverse norm at most A=2A_0. Since B_{n,s},r_H,r_K are finite, arbitrarily small nonzero ε meet every inequality.

For s≥n+3 the weighted Fourier convolution estimate makes H^s an algebra; Cauchy–Schwarz gives convergence of the Fourier series and of the required differentiated series. Applying these facts to the finite Hessian polynomial gives the constants C_{n,s},D_{n,s}, with a uniform C_{n,s} on the fixed ε interval. Factoring each polynomial difference supplies the displayed Lipschitz estimate. Each term has zero integral by Stokes against δ(k^{n−r})=0. These are expanded coefficient and positivity estimates, not assumptions of existence. With the stated R, the map w↦L_ε^−1(g−Q_ε(w)) maps the radius-R ball into itself and contracts by at most 1/2, as proved in w7-1/n7. For g=cf−f_ε its mean is zero and its norm meets the stated bound. Iteration yields w with the asserted equation and k+δw≥K_0/4.

All hypotheses of w7-1/n7 have now been verified. Its proof yields a genuine continuous descent u with finite canonical values and the prescribed normalization. More importantly, its mass argument applies to every bounded genuine canonical competitor, and its energy argument compares any such competitor with the strictly positive constructed solution. Thus all competitors have mass M, every equation constant is c=M/ν(X), and any two solutions differ by a constant at every point. This is uniqueness in ordinary type zero, the entire bounded class, not just in the contraction ball or among smooth functions. Bounded local truncations are stationary, so these statements concern the task's extended non-pluripolar products. The local non-pluripolarity proof also gives finiteness and non-pluripolarity of ν.

Actual descent is particularly transparent here. π is a homeomorphism, and each disk has a unique holomorphic lift. For every such lift and every prescribed local p_{f_0},
δ(U∘f̃_0+p_{f_0})=f̃_0*(H+δU)≥0.
The continuous values are therefore the genuine canonical values, not alterations on a null set. The inverse cusp estimate follows by distinguishing |z+z′|≥|z−z′|/2 from its complement: in the first case the quadratic difference controls |z−z′|³ on a bounded chart, and in the second the cubic difference is at least |z−z′|³/16. Bedford–Taylor, Acta Mathematica 149 (1982), uses D=2i∂bar∂.
